ayyubid-emirate-of-mayyafariqin.t: The Ayyubid principality of Diyar Bakr, whose last prince died resisting the Mongols after a long siege in 1260.
ayyubid-emirate-of-mayyafariqin.o: Saladin took Mayyafariqin in 1185 from the Shah-Armens' sphere and gave it to his brother al-Adil, whose son al-Awhad Ayyub ruled it and in 1207 took Ahlat. It became a hereditary Ayyubid principality in the Jazira.
ayyubid-emirate-of-mayyafariqin.r: The principality passed to al-Ashraf Musa and then to al-Muzaffar Ghazi, sons of al-Adil, and then to Ghazi's son al-Kamil Muhammad. Its rulers controlled the old Marwanid capital, rich farmland north of the Tigris and roads to Ahlat. They faced the Khwarazmians, the Sultanate of Rum and finally the Mongols. Al-Kamil Muhammad defied Hulagu.
ayyubid-emirate-of-mayyafariqin.e: Mongol forces besieged Mayyafariqin from 1259; in 1260 the city fell after famine, al-Kamil Muhammad was killed and his head was paraded in Syrian cities.

aspendos.t: Aspendos, a wealthy Pamphylian city on the Eurymedon river, near which Athens defeated Persia and later the Romans built a famous theatre.
aspendos.o: Aspendos rose on a hill by the Eurymedon river, a few kilometres from the sea, in the 7th century BCE. Its people claimed descent from settlers from Argos, but its coins were inscribed in the local Pamphylian Greek dialect with the name Estwediiys.
aspendos.r: The city prospered from horse breeding, farming and salt and river trade, and minted silver coins. Around 466 BCE the Athenian general Cimon defeated a Persian fleet and army near the Eurymedon. In 333 BCE Aspendos submitted to Alexander, who demanded tribute and horses after it reneged on terms.
aspendos.e: Aspendos passed under Seleucid and Pergamene influence, then Roman rule, joining the province of Galatia in 25 BCE. Its theatre, built in the 2nd century CE, is one of the best preserved from antiquity.

archbishopric-of-riga.t: Ecclesiastical principality that led the Christian conquest of Livonia and governed much of Latvia for nearly four centuries.
archbishopric-of-riga.o: The missionary Meinhard became bishop of the Livs at Üxküll in 1186. His successor Albert of Buxhoeveden founded Riga in 1201 and moved the see there, directing the crusade with the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. In 1255 Riga was raised to an archbishopric under Albert Suerbeer, with authority over the bishoprics of Livonia and Prussia.
archbishopric-of-riga.r: The archbishops were princes of the Holy Roman Empire, ruling lands along the Daugava and Gauja through vassals and castles such as Turaida and Kokenhusen. Their rule was marked by long conflicts with the Livonian Order and with the citizens of Riga over control of the city. The cathedral chapter and vassals sat in the Livonian diets.
archbishopric-of-riga.e: The Reformation reached Riga in the 1520s, weakening the archbishops. During the Livonian War the last archbishop, Wilhelm of Brandenburg, placed his lands under Polish-Lithuanian protection, and in 1561-1562 they were secularised and incorporated into the Duchy of Livonia under Sigismund II Augustus.

ancient-shu.t: The early kingdom of the Sichuan basin, heir to the astonishing bronze culture of Sanxingdui, conquered by Qin in 316 BCE.
ancient-shu.o: Shu emerged in the Chengdu plain from a long local tradition: the Sanxingdui culture, with its giant bronze masks and standing figure, and the later Jinsha site in Chengdu. Later legends name a series of kings, Cancong, Yufu and Duyu, followed by the Kaiming dynasty, but these accounts were written centuries afterwards.
ancient-shu.r: Shu developed largely independently of the Zhou states, and its bronze art, sun worship and burial customs, including boat-shaped coffins, differ sharply from those of northern China. Under the Kaiming kings it was centred on Chengdu and was rich in rice, salt and copper. It had no widely used script; the so-called Ba-Shu signs remain undeciphered.
ancient-shu.e: Quarrels between Shu and the neighbouring State of Ba gave the State of Qin a pretext; in 316 BCE the Qin general Sima Cuo conquered Shu. Qin settled colonists there, and the governor Li Bing built the Dujiangyan irrigation system, making Sichuan the granary that fuelled Qin's unification of China.

areopagus-of-eastern-continental-greece.t: Regional revolutionary government of eastern mainland Greece in 1821-1822, set up at Salona under Theodoros Negris.
areopagus-of-eastern-continental-greece.o: Eastern mainland Greece, including Attica, Boeotia, Phocis and Locris, joined the revolution in 1821. In November 1821 an assembly of local representatives met at Salona (Amfissa) and, under the guidance of the Phanariot diplomat Theodoros Negris, adopted a legal charter and created a governing council named after the ancient Athenian Areopagus.
areopagus-of-eastern-continental-greece.r: The Areopagus was made up of local notables and was meant to run the administration, justice and war effort in the region. It struggled to control powerful armed chieftains, above all Odysseas Androutsos, with whom it was in open conflict. Its authority over the scattered and contested territory was limited.
areopagus-of-eastern-continental-greece.e: After the First National Assembly at Epidaurus created the First Hellenic Republic in January 1822, the regional bodies were subordinated to central government. The Areopagus continued for a time but lost its role during 1822 and 1823.

akusha-dargo-union.t: A powerful union of self-governing Dargin communities in central Dagestan, led by the qadi of Akusha, which long resisted both khans and Russia.
akusha-dargo-union.o: The Dargin highlands of central Dagestan were home to free communities, called jamaats, that governed themselves without princes. By the 17th century the largest of them formed a union around the village of Akusha, whose qadi, a religious judge, served as its leading authority.
akusha-dargo-union.r: The union was a confederation of village communities with their own assemblies and customary law, coordinated by the qadi and councils of elders. It could field several thousand warriors and was among the strongest forces in Dagestan. Its people farmed terraced fields, herded sheep and were known for metalworking in villages such as Kubachi nearby.
akusha-dargo-union.e: General Yermolov defeated the Akusha forces at Levashi in 1819 and imposed Russian authority. The union was finally incorporated into the Russian Empire in 1844 amid the wars of the Caucasian Imamate.

andecavi.t: Gallic people of Anjou whose leader Dumnacus fought one of the last campaigns against Rome in 51 BCE.
andecavi.o: The Andecavi, called Andes by Caesar, lived on the lower Loire around Angers. Caesar quartered legions among them in 57 BCE and records that they joined the revolt of 52 BCE.
andecavi.r: Little is known of their institutions beyond their war leaders.
andecavi.e: In 51 BCE Dumnacus besieged the pro-Roman Pictones in Lemonum, but was defeated by Caesar's legate Gaius Fabius and fled. Under Rome their chief town was Juliomagus, later called Andecavi, the origin of Angers and of the name Anjou.

archchancellors-electorate.t: State created for Karl Theodor von Dalberg, the last Archbishop of Mainz, to keep the imperial archchancellor's office alive.
archchancellors-electorate.o: When the left bank of the Rhine passed to France, the Electorate of Mainz lost its capital. The Imperial Recess of 1803 kept its archbishop, Karl Theodor von Dalberg, as elector and archchancellor of the Empire, and gave him the Principality of Aschaffenburg, Regensburg and the County of Wetzlar, with the archiepiscopal seat moved to Regensburg.
archchancellors-electorate.r: Dalberg was an Enlightenment churchman who governed from Regensburg, seat of the Perpetual Imperial Diet. His state was scattered and Catholic, with Aschaffenburg as its richest part. He cultivated Napoleon, praising him as a new Charlemagne, and in 1806 became Prince-Primate of the Confederation of the Rhine, adding Frankfurt to his lands.
archchancellors-electorate.e: In 1810 Dalberg ceded Regensburg to the Kingdom of Bavaria and in exchange received Hanau and Fulda, creating the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt. Dalberg remained its ruler until 1813, and Regensburg has belonged to Bavaria ever since.

anconine-republic.t: A short-lived French-backed republic in the Adriatic port of Ancona, carved from the Papal States in 1797 and merged into the Roman Republic.
anconine-republic.o: French troops occupied Ancona, the main Adriatic port of the Papal States, in February 1797, and the Treaty of Tolentino left them in control of it. In November 1797 local patriots, with French encouragement, proclaimed the Anconine Republic, with jurisdiction over Ancona and nearby towns of the Marche.
anconine-republic.r: The republic was governed by a provisional administration of local Jacobins under French military control. It abolished the old papal institutions, freed the city's Jews from the ghetto restrictions and adopted French-style laws and symbols. It also served as a base for French plans against the rest of the Papal States.
anconine-republic.e: When French troops occupied Rome and created the Roman Republic (1798–1799) in February 1798, the Anconine Republic was absorbed into it in March 1798.

astures.t: The peoples of Asturias and León, last in Iberia to fall to Rome in 19 BCE, whose land became the empire's great gold-mining district.
astures.o: The Astures occupied the lands between the Cantabrian coast and the Douro, in modern Asturias, León and northern Zamora, from about the 4th century BCE. Romans divided them into the Transmontani north of the mountains and the Augustani on the plateau to the south.
astures.r: They lived in castros, fortified hilltop villages of round stone houses, in many independent communities grouped by kinship. Herding, farming and metalworking supported them, and their mountains held rich gold deposits. Their main stronghold on the plain was Lancia, near León. They spoke a Celtic language.
astures.e: The Astures fought alongside the Cantabri in Augustus' Cantabrian Wars of 29 to 19 BCE. After conquest Rome founded Asturica Augusta (Astorga) and exploited the gold of Las Médulas on a vast scale. Their name survives in Asturias and in the later Kingdom of Asturias.

alba-longa.t: Legendary mother city of the Latins in the Alban Hills, remembered by the Romans as the home of Romulus and Remus and the seat of the Latin festival.
alba-longa.o: Roman tradition held that Ascanius, son of the Trojan hero Aeneas, founded Alba Longa about thirty years after Lavinium, and placed its foundation in the 12th century BCE. Archaeology shows Iron Age villages and cemeteries around the Alban Lake and Monte Cavo from about 1000 BCE, but no single city has been firmly identified.
alba-longa.r: The Romans described a line of Alban kings, from Silvius to Numitor and his usurping brother Amulius, but these are legendary. What is more secure is the role of the Alban Hills as a religious centre for the Latin peoples: the sanctuary of Jupiter Latiaris on Monte Cavo hosted the Feriae Latinae, a shared festival that Rome kept celebrating long after Alba disappeared.
alba-longa.e: According to Livy, Rome under Tullus Hostilius defeated Alba after the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii in the mid-7th century BCE, razed the city and moved its people to the Caelian Hill. Leading Roman families such as the Julii claimed Alban descent, and the Latin League inherited its religious role.

antes.t: An early Slavic people between the Dniester and the Dnieper, known from Byzantine writers as raiders and allies of the 6th-century empire.
antes.o: The Antes appear in the 6th century in Procopius and Jordanes, who describe them as a people related to the Sclaveni living east of the Dniester. Archaeologists usually connect them with the Penkovka culture. Jordanes also tells how an Antian leader named Boz was killed by the Goths, but the story is hard to date.
antes.r: Procopius says the Antes were not ruled by one man but lived in a kind of democracy, deciding matters in common, and worshipped a god of lightning as lord of all. They farmed, kept livestock and lived in scattered villages. From the 530s they raided the Balkans, but Justinian also hired them as allies to guard the Danube.
antes.e: The Avars attacked them in the 560s, and an Avar expedition sent against them in 602 is the last time the Antes are mentioned. Their people were absorbed into the East Slavic tribes of later centuries, while the title Anticus lingered for a time in the Byzantine emperor's style.

argentine-republic.t: The republic reunited under Buenos Aires in 1861, which became one of the world's richest countries by 1900 before a century of political turmoil.
argentine-republic.o: After Bartolomé Mitre's victory at Pavón in 1861 over the Argentine Confederation, Buenos Aires and the provinces were reunited under the Constitution of 1853, as amended in 1860, which adopted the name Argentine Republic. Mitre became president in 1862.
argentine-republic.r: Mitre, Domingo Sarmiento and Nicolás Avellaneda built national institutions and schools. Argentina fought Paraguay from 1865 to 1870, and Julio Argentino Roca's Conquest of the Desert seized the pampas and Patagonia. Mass immigration from Italy and Spain and exports of beef and wheat made it among the world's richest countries by 1914. A military coup in 1930 began decades of instability. Juan Perón led a powerful labour-based movement from 1946.
argentine-republic.e: The dictatorship of 1976 to 1983 killed thousands in the Dirty War and lost the Falklands War. Democracy returned in 1983 under Raúl Alfonsín. Repeated economic crises, including a default in 2001, followed, and Javier Milei was elected in 2023.

aram-zobah.t: Aram-Zobah, an Aramaean kingdom of the 10th century BCE, the main rival of King David in the Bible.
aram-zobah.o: Zobah was an Aramaean kingdom probably centred on the Beqaa valley and the region north of Damascus. It is known almost entirely from the Hebrew Bible, which describes its king Hadadezer son of Rehob as a powerful ruler whose influence reached the Euphrates.
aram-zobah.r: According to the Bible, Hadadezer commanded chariots and allied Aramaean kingdoms, and rich towns of his land produced bronze. Little else is known, since no inscriptions from Zobah have been found.
aram-zobah.e: The Bible says David of the United Kingdom of Israel defeated Hadadezer and took his gold shields to Jerusalem, and that Rezon, a former officer, founded Aram-Damascus, which soon replaced Zobah as the leading Aramaean power.

aenus.t: Aeolian city at the mouth of the Hebrus river in Thrace, a gateway for trade with the Thracian interior.
aenus.o: Aenus was founded by Aeolian settlers from Mytilene and Cyme on a hill at the mouth of the Hebrus, the modern Maritsa or Evros, on the Thracian coast. Homer mentions a Thracian named from Aenus, and the city flourished from the 6th century BCE.
aenus.r: Aenus traded salt fish and goods with the Thracian interior along the Hebrus, including the Odrysian Kingdom. It struck fine silver coins with the head of Hermes. Aenus paid tribute in the Delian League and fought on the Athenian side at Syracuse in 413 BCE.
aenus.e: In the Hellenistic period Aenus was held in turn by the Ptolemaic Empire and the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia. Rome declared it free in 167 BCE, and it came under Roman control by 146 BCE. It is today the Turkish town of Enez.

andros.t: Northernmost large island of the Cyclades, coloniser of the Chalcidice and remembered for defying Themistocles's demand for money in 480 BCE.
andros.o: Andros, just south-east of Euboea, was settled by Ionian Greeks in the early Iron Age. The fortified Geometric town of Zagora flourished in the 8th century BCE. Andros was long linked with Eretria, and c. 655 BCE Andrians founded colonies in the Chalcidice, including Acanthus, Stagira and Argilus.
andros.r: The island lived from farming, wine and seafaring. It sent ships to Xerxes in 480 BCE; when Themistocles demanded money, the Andrians replied that their gods were Poverty and Helplessness. Andros later paid tribute in the Delian League, and Athens planted a colony there c. 450 BCE. The marble Hermes of Andros shows its later prosperity.
andros.e: Under Hellenistic kings Andros changed hands often. Rome captured it in 199 BCE and handed it to Attalus I of the Kingdom of Pergamon, and it passed to direct Roman control after 133 BCE.

arcadian-league.t: Short-lived federation of the Arcadian cities created after Leuctra, which built Megalopolis and helped break Spartan power in the Peloponnese.
arcadian-league.o: Sparta's defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE freed the Arcadians to act together. Led by Lycomedes of Mantinea and backed by Thebes, they formed a federal state in 370 BCE, and Mantinea was refounded. A new federal capital, Megalopolis, was built by uniting dozens of villages in south-western Arcadia.
arcadian-league.r: The league had an assembly known as the Ten Thousand, a federal council and magistrates, and a standing elite force, the eparitoi, paid from federal funds. It joined Thebes in invading Laconia and supported the refounding of Messene. Arcadian pride and a sense of common identity were expressed in federal coins and dedications.
arcadian-league.e: Quarrels with Elis led the Arcadians to seize Olympia, and disputes over using the sanctuary's treasure to pay the eparitoi split the league in 363 BCE, with Mantinea siding with Sparta and Tegea with Thebes. The Battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE left the federation broken, though Megalopolis endured.

albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.t: Albania under Italian occupation, joined to Italy in a personal union under King Victor Emmanuel III and used as a base for the invasion of Greece.
albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.o: Italy invaded Albania on 7 April 1939, forcing King Zog of the Albanian Kingdom into exile. A constituent assembly summoned in Tirana offered the crown to Victor Emmanuel III, creating a personal union with Italy. Shefqet Vërlaci, a large landowner and rival of Zog, became prime minister under an Italian lieutenant-general, Francesco Jacomoni.
albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.r: Real power lay with Italian officials: Albania's army and foreign service were merged into Italy's and an Albanian Fascist Party was created. Italy launched its invasion of Greece from Albanian soil in October 1940, and after the conquest of Yugoslavia in 1941 Kosovo and western Macedonia were added, forming a Greater Albania. Resistance grew, including Enver Hoxha's Communist Party, founded in 1941.
albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.e: When Italy capitulated in September 1943, German troops occupied Albania and created the Albanian Kingdom (1943-1944), a nominally independent state under German control. Victor Emmanuel III formally renounced the Albanian crown in 1943, and the union with Italy was never restored.
albanian-kingdom-1939-1943.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

appenzell-innerrhoden.t: The Catholic half of Appenzell, created by the canton's division in 1597, which still governs itself by an open-air assembly.
appenzell-innerrhoden.o: In 1597 the Canton of Appenzell, divided by the Reformation, was split in two with the mediation of the other Swiss cantons. The Catholic inner districts around the village of Appenzell formed Innerrhoden, keeping the old seat and archives.
appenzell-innerrhoden.r: Innerrhoden governed itself through its Landsgemeinde, meeting in the square at Appenzell, which elected the Landammann and passed laws. It shared a single vote in the federal Diet with Ausserrhoden. The economy rested on cattle and dairy farming and later on embroidery done at home. Capuchin friars strengthened the Counter-Reformation.
appenzell-innerrhoden.e: The French invasion of 1798 merged Appenzell into the canton of Säntis of the Helvetic Republic. Restored in 1803, Innerrhoden still holds its Landsgemeinde; it was the last canton to give women the vote, in 1990, after a federal court ruling.

aland.t: Demilitarised, Swedish-speaking island autonomy within Finland, created by a League of Nations decision in 1921 and still self-governing today.
aland.o: The Åland Islands, between Sweden and Finland, passed to Russia with Finland in 1809 and were demilitarised after the Crimean War in 1856. When Finland became independent, most Ålanders, who speak Swedish, wanted to join Sweden. The League of Nations ruled in 1921 that the islands belonged to Finland, but with guaranteed autonomy and protection of the Swedish language.
aland.r: Åland governs itself through its own parliament, the Lagting, first convened in 1922 under Julius Sundblom, and a government in Mariehamn, with powers over education, culture, policing and local economy. Swedish is the only official language, and the right of domicile restricts land ownership to residents. The islands remain demilitarised and neutral, and their economy rests on shipping, ferries and tourism.
aland.e: Autonomy has been widened by later acts, and Åland gained its own flag in 1954 and its own stamps in 1984. When Finland joined the EU in 1995, Åland kept a special status outside the EU tax area. It remains an autonomous region of the Republic of Finland.

ahhiyawa.t: A Late Bronze Age power named in some thirty Hittite texts, widely identified with the Mycenaean Greeks, the Achaeans of Homer.
ahhiyawa.o: The name Ahhiyawa, close to Homer's Achaeans, appears in Hittite records from c. 1400 BCE, when a 'man of Ahhiya' named Attarissiya raided western Anatolia and Alashiya. Most scholars now accept that it denotes a Mycenaean Greek kingdom, or a coalition of them, though its centre is debated, with Mycenae, Thebes and Rhodes all proposed.
ahhiyawa.r: In the 13th century BCE a Hittite king addressed the king of Ahhiyawa as a 'Great King' and 'brother', ranking him with Egypt, Babylon and Assyria. Ahhiyawa held Millawanda on the Anatolian coast and backed rebels such as Piyamaradu. Hittite texts mention ships from Ahhiyawa and a dispute over Wilusa, often linked with Troy.
ahhiyawa.e: In a treaty of Tudhaliya IV, c. 1230 BCE, the king of Ahhiyawa was struck from the list of great kings, suggesting its power had waned. References cease soon after, as the Mycenaean palaces collapsed c. 1200 BCE.

ayyubid-emirate-of-hama.t: The longest-surviving Ayyubid principality, which lasted under Mamluk overlordship and was ruled by the historian and geographer Abu al-Fida.
ayyubid-emirate-of-hama.o: In 1178 Saladin granted Hama on the Orontes to his nephew Taqi al-Din Umar, whose descendants kept it as a hereditary principality within the Ayyubid family confederation.
ayyubid-emirate-of-hama.r: Hama's rulers usually sided with the sultans in Egypt against their cousins in Damascus and Aleppo. Al-Mansur Muhammad II joined the Mamluks against the Mongols in 1260 and was allowed to keep his throne as a vassal. The principality was known for its learned princes: Abu al-Fida, appointed ruler in 1310 by the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, wrote a universal history and the geographical work Taqwim al-Buldan. The great waterwheels of the Orontes irrigated its gardens.
ayyubid-emirate-of-hama.e: After Abu al-Fida's death in 1331, his son al-Afdal Muhammad was deposed in 1341, and Hama became an ordinary Mamluk province.

archbishopric-of-magdeburg.t: Otto the Great's favoured archbishopric on the Elbe, head of the church in the Slavic east, which became a Protestant territory and then part of Brandenburg-Prussia.
archbishopric-of-magdeburg.o: Otto I founded a monastery at Magdeburg in 937 and, after years of negotiation with the Pope and the Archbishop of Mainz, raised it to an archbishopric in 968, with suffragans at Merseburg, Meissen, Zeitz (later Naumburg), Brandenburg and Havelberg. Otto and his first wife, Edith of England, are buried in the cathedral.
archbishopric-of-magdeburg.r: The archbishops ruled a territory along the middle Elbe and Saale. Archbishop Wichmann granted Magdeburg its town law around 1188, a model copied across central and eastern Europe. The Gothic cathedral, begun in 1209, was the first in Germany. Albert of Brandenburg's sale of indulgences as archbishop prompted Luther's theses in 1517.
archbishopric-of-magdeburg.e: Magdeburg became Lutheran, ruled by Protestant administrators, and the city was sacked by imperial troops in 1631. The Peace of Westphalia assigned the archbishopric to Brandenburg on the death of its administrator, which happened in 1680, when it became the Duchy of Magdeburg within Brandenburg-Prussia.

abdera-800.t: A Phoenician trading port on the coast of Almería, at modern Adra, that later minted coins under Carthaginian and Roman rule.
abdera-800.o: Phoenician settlers founded Abdera in the 8th century BCE on the hill of Montecristo at modern Adra, at the mouth of the river Adra. It was one of a chain of Phoenician harbours along the southern coast of Iberia, with Sexi and Malaka, linking Gadir with the eastern Mediterranean.
abdera-800.r: Little is known of its government. Like its neighbours, Abdera lived from trade with the Iberian hinterland, fishing and the salting of fish. In the Punic period it fell under the influence of Carthage, and its later coins, inscribed in Punic letters, showed a temple facade with tuna fish.
abdera-800.e: After the Roman victory over Carthage in Hispania in 206 BCE Abdera came under Rome, keeping its coinage into the early empire. It continued as a small Roman town, and Strabo listed it among the Phoenician foundations of the coast.

argos.t: Ancient city of the Argolid, Sparta's enduring rival in the Peloponnese, famed for the sanctuary of Hera and the sculptor Polykleitos.
argos.o: Argos lies in the Argive plain below the Larisa and Aspis hills and was inhabited from the Bronze Age. In the early Iron Age Dorian settlers made it the leading city of the Argolid. In the 7th century BCE King Pheidon, credited with standard measures, made it the strongest power in the Peloponnese, and Argos beat Sparta at Hysiai c. 669 BCE.
argos.r: Argos controlled the great Heraion between it and Mycenae and was a centre of bronze sculpture, home of Hageladas and Polykleitos. Its power was broken when Cleomenes I of Sparta destroyed its army at Sepeia c. 494 BCE. Argos stayed neutral in 480 BCE, then destroyed Mycenae and Tiryns and adopted democracy.
argos.e: Allied with Athens, Argos was defeated at Mantinea in 418 BCE. Pyrrhus of the Kingdom of Epirus died fighting in its streets in 272 BCE. Argos joined the Achaean League in 229 BCE and passed under Rome in 146 BCE.

aduatuci.t: Belgic people said to descend from Cimbri and Teutones, whose entire population was sold into slavery by Caesar in 57 BCE.
aduatuci.o: Caesar says the Aduatuci descended from six thousand Cimbri and Teutones left to guard the baggage of the great migration before 102 BCE, who settled on the middle Meuse. Their stronghold is usually placed near Namur or Thuin in Belgium.
aduatuci.r: They imposed tribute on their neighbours, including the Eburones, and fortified a hilltop oppidum.
aduatuci.e: In 57 BCE they surrendered to Caesar but attacked his camp at night with hidden weapons. Caesar stormed the oppidum and sold the inhabitants, fifty-three thousand by his count, into slavery. Survivors joined Ambiorix in 54 BCE, after which the name disappears.

aedui.t: Leading people of central Gaul and Rome's oldest Gallic ally, whose quarrels with their rivals gave Caesar his pretext to invade Gaul.
aedui.o: The Aedui held the land between the Loire and the Saône, in modern Burgundy, with their great oppidum at Bibracte on Mont Beuvray. By the 2nd century BCE they were hailed by the Roman Senate as brothers and kinsmen of the Roman people, and they contested leadership of Gaul with the Arverni and the Sequani.
aedui.r: Government was oligarchic: a council of nobles and an annual chief magistrate, the vergobret, who could not leave the territory during office. Bibracte was a large town of craftsmen, enamellers and traders importing Italian wine. The druid Diviciacus spoke for Rome in the Senate, while his brother Dumnorix led the anti-Roman party.
aedui.e: Pressed by the Sequani and Ariovistus, the Aedui called on Caesar in 58 BCE, but in 52 BCE they joined Vercingetorix, who was chosen supreme leader at Bibracte. Pardoned after Alesia, they moved to the new city of Augustodunum (Autun), and in 48 CE Claudius admitted Aeduan nobles to the Roman Senate.

atrebates.t: Belgic people of Artois whose king Commius served Caesar, then turned against him and founded a dynasty in Britain.
atrebates.o: The Atrebates lived in the modern Artois around Nemetocenna (Arras). They joined the Belgic league in 57 BCE, promising fifteen thousand men, and fought beside the Nervii at the Sabis.
atrebates.r: After their defeat Caesar made Commius their king and used him as an envoy to the Britons in 55 BCE, extending his authority over the Morini. Their coins and their links across the Channel show close ties with Britain, where a people of the same name lived.
atrebates.e: Commius joined the great revolt of 52 BCE, helped lead the relief army at Alesia and later fled to Britain, where coins name his successors among the British Atrebates. Under Rome Nemetocenna became a civitas capital, the origin of Arras, and the name survives in Artois.

acragas.t: Greek city of south-west Sicily, famed for its temples and wealth, home of the philosopher Empedocles, which Pindar called the most beautiful city of mortals.
acragas.o: Colonists from Gela, with Rhodians, founded Acragas around 580 BCE on a ridge above the confluence of the Akragas and Hypsas rivers, near Sicily's south coast. Within a few decades it was one of the largest Greek cities.
acragas.r: The tyrant Phalaris, notorious for roasting enemies in a bronze bull, ruled around 570–554 BCE. Under Theron, who with Gelon defeated Carthage at Himera in 480 BCE, Acragas grew rich on grain, olives and trade with Carthage. Prisoners built temples along the southern ridge, today's Valley of the Temples, including the Temple of Concord and the colossal Olympieion. The philosopher Empedocles helped restore democracy there.
acragas.e: Carthage sacked Acragas in 406 BCE. Revived by Timoleon, it was taken by Rome in 262 BCE, retaken by Carthage, and finally captured by Rome in 210 BCE, becoming Agrigentum. The modern city, Agrigento, overlooks the temples, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

alawi-sheikhdom.t: One of the smallest states of the Aden Protectorate, a tribal sheikhdom near the Yemeni frontier.
alawi-sheikhdom.o: The Alawi sheikhdom was a small tribal territory in the hills north of Aden, near Dhala, with its seat at Al Qasha. Like its neighbours, it gained independence in the 18th century as the Qasimid State withdrew from the south. Its early history is barely recorded.
alawi-sheikhdom.r: The sheikhs ruled a few thousand people by tribal custom. The territory entered British protection through treaties in the late 19th century and was part of the Western Aden Protectorate. In 1965 it joined the Federation of South Arabia, the British-sponsored union of protectorate states.
alawi-sheikhdom.e: After the National Liberation Front took power in 1967, the sheikhdom was abolished and absorbed into South Yemen.

atrebates-britain.t: Southern British kingdom founded by the Gallic exile Commius, whose last king Verica fled to Rome and gave Claudius his pretext for invasion in 43.
atrebates-britain.o: Commius, king of the Atrebates of northern Gaul, first served Julius Caesar and then joined the Gallic revolt of 52 BCE. Around 50 BCE he fled across the Channel, and coins bearing his name soon appear in central southern Britain, where he appears to have founded a dynasty ruling Hampshire, Berkshire and Sussex.
atrebates-britain.r: Kings claiming descent from Commius, notably Tincomarus, Eppillus and Verica, issued gold coins that increasingly copied Roman designs, and Verica's carry a vine leaf and the title REX, signs of friendship with Rome. Calleva, the later Silchester, grew into a planned oppidum with imported wine, olive oil and tableware. Pressure from the Catuvellauni under Cunobelinus and his sons steadily shrank the kingdom.
atrebates-britain.e: Around 41 or 42 Verica was driven out and went to Rome to seek help, which Claudius used to justify the invasion of 43. Afterwards much of the territory passed to the client Kingdom of the Regni under Togidubnus, and Calleva Atrebatum became a civitas capital of Roman Britain.

agathyrsi.t: Gold-rich people of Transylvania described by Herodotus, known for tattoos, luxury and refusing to join the Scythians against Persia.
agathyrsi.o: Herodotus places the Agathyrsi along the Maris (Mureș) in Transylvania in the 6th century BCE. Their origins are debated: they may have been a Scythian-influenced elite over a Thracian population, and Greek myth made their founder Agathyrsus a son of Heracles.
agathyrsi.r: Herodotus describes them as wearing much gold, tattooing themselves and holding wives in common so that all would be kin. Their king Spargapeithes killed the Scythian king Ariapeithes. When Darius I invaded Scythia around 513 BCE, they refused Scythian refugees entry to their land. Scythian-style graves in Transylvania are often linked to them.
agathyrsi.e: After the 5th century BCE they vanish from the record; their lands later appear as part of the territory of the Getae and Dacians, into whom they were probably absorbed.

ayyubid-emirate-of-damascus.t: The Ayyubid principality of Damascus after Saladin, a prize fought over by his brothers, sons and grandsons until the Mongols arrived in 1260.
ayyubid-emirate-of-damascus.o: When Saladin died in Damascus in 1193, his empire was divided among his sons, and Damascus went to the eldest, al-Afdal Ali. In 1196 his uncle al-Adil and brother al-Aziz drove him out, and Damascus passed to al-Adil's line.
ayyubid-emirate-of-damascus.r: Damascus was the richest prize in Syria and the seat of a scholarly and religious elite. Al-Mu'azzam Isa (1218-1227), a Hanafi jurist, built schools and dismantled the walls of Jerusalem in 1219 to keep them from the Crusaders. Later princes, al-Nasir Dawud, al-Ashraf Musa and al-Salih Ismail, fought the sultans in Egypt; al-Salih Ismail even ceded castles to the Franks. Al-Salih Ayyub took the city in 1245.
ayyubid-emirate-of-damascus.e: Al-Nasir Yusuf of the Ayyubid Emirate of Aleppo seized Damascus in 1250. The Mongols occupied it in March 1260, and after their defeat at Ain Jalut it passed to the Mamluks.

afrighid-khwarazm.t: The native dynasty of Khwarazm for nearly seven centuries, whose shahs kept the region's Iranian culture alive through Arab conquest and Samanid overlordship.
afrighid-khwarazm.o: According to the Khwarazmian scholar al-Biruni, the Afrighid dynasty was founded by Afrig in 305 CE, succeeding the older royal house of the Kingdom of Khwarazm. Afrig built a fortress at Kath on the Amu Darya, which became the capital.
afrighid-khwarazm.r: The shahs ruled an irrigated land of canals, towns and fortified manors that traded north with the steppe and the Volga. Zoroastrianism and the Khwarazmian language and calendar persisted. After the Arab general Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered Khwarazm in 712, the shahs remained as vassals, converted to Islam and ruled under Caliphal and later Samanid authority, while a rival centre grew at Gurganj.
afrighid-khwarazm.e: In 995 the emir of Gurganj, Ma'mun ibn Muhammad, overthrew and killed the last Afrighid shah, Abu Abdallah Muhammad, and founded Ma'munid Khwarazm. Al-Biruni, born near Kath, preserved much of what is known of the dynasty.

aegina.t: Island state in the Saronic Gulf that minted some of the first Greek coins and was the great commercial rival of Athens until 431 BCE.
aegina.o: Aegina, an island between Attica and the Argolid, was settled from the Neolithic and had a strong Bronze Age town at Kolonna. In the early Iron Age it was resettled by Dorians from Epidaurus, and by the 7th century BCE it had become one of the busiest trading states of the Greek world.
aegina.r: Aegina struck silver 'turtle' coins from c. 550 BCE, and its weight standard spread across much of Greece. Its merchants traded at Naucratis in Egypt, and its oligarchic elite built the temple of Aphaia, whose pediment sculptures are now in Munich. Aegina gave earth and water to Persia in 491 BCE, but its ships won the prize for valour at Salamis in 480 BCE.
aegina.e: Long wars with Athens ended in 457 BCE, when Aegina was forced into the Delian League. In 431 BCE Athens expelled the Aeginetans and settled colonists; Sparta gave the exiles land at Thyrea. Lysander restored survivors in 405 BCE, but the island never regained its former power.

abrincatui.t: Small Gallic people of the bay of Mont Saint-Michel, whose name survives in the town of Avranches.
abrincatui.o: Known only from Pliny, Ptolemy and later Roman records, the Abrincatui held the southern end of the Cotentin coast on the border of Normandy and Brittany. They were neighbours of the Unelli and Redones and were probably dependents of a larger Armorican people.
abrincatui.r: Nothing is recorded of their institutions. Ptolemy names their town Ingena, generally placed at Avranches.
abrincatui.e: They were drawn into the Roman conquest of Armorica in 57 and 56 BCE. Under Rome they formed a small civitas in Gallia Lugdunensis whose chief town took the people's name as Abrincatae, the origin of Avranches, later a bishopric.

abadzekhs.t: A self-governing Circassian people of the forested foothills of the western Caucasus, among the most determined opponents of the Russian conquest.
abadzekhs.o: The Abadzekhs inhabited the forested valleys of the upper Belaya, Pshish and Psekups rivers, behind the coastal Shapsugs. They emerged as a distinct and numerous Adyghe community of Circassia by the 17th century; earlier history is not separately recorded. Their villages lay scattered in clearings across the forest.
abadzekhs.r: Like the Shapsugs and Natukhaj, they shed the authority of princes in the late 18th century and governed through assemblies and customary law, with sworn associations of households. They lived by farming, herding and forest crafts. From 1848 Muhammad Amin, Shamil's envoy, organised them into a more centralised Islamic administration with courts and taxes.
abadzekhs.e: The Abadzekhs submitted to Russia in 1859 but soon resumed resistance. The Russian Empire completed the conquest in 1864, and the great majority were expelled to the Ottoman Empire. A few villages remained near Maykop, in what is now Adygea.

ashkelon.t: Ashkelon, the Philistine seaport of the southern Levant, whose Iron Age cemetery has revealed the Aegean origins of its settlers.
ashkelon.o: Ashkelon had been a large Canaanite harbour town since the Middle Bronze Age, and its kings wrote to Egypt in the Amarna letters. In the 12th century BCE Philistines settled there, and it became one of the cities of the Philistine Pentapolis.
ashkelon.r: Its kings ruled a busy port trading wine and oil, with a market in the city centre. Excavations led by Lawrence Stager uncovered a Philistine cemetery, and a 2019 DNA study found that its early inhabitants included newcomers of southern European ancestry. King Sidqa rebelled against Sennacherib in 701 BCE and was deported.
ashkelon.e: Ashkelon remained an Assyrian vassal until Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire destroyed it in 604 BCE and deported its king Aga to Babylon. The city later revived as a Phoenician and Greek port.

armenian-principality-of-cilicia.t: A mountain principality founded by Armenian refugees and nobles in the Taurus, which grew into the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia and allied with the Crusaders.
armenian-principality-of-cilicia.o: After the Byzantine defeat at Manzikert in 1071 and the loss of Armenian lands to the Seljuks, Armenian lords established themselves in the Taurus mountains of Cilicia. Around 1080 Ruben, a follower of the last Bagratid king, created a lordship that became the base of the Rubenid dynasty.
armenian-principality-of-cilicia.r: Lords ruled from fortresses such as Vahka and later the plain cities of Sis and Anazarbus. Thoros I took the Cilician plain from Byzantium, and the Rubenids cooperated with the Crusader states of Antioch and Edessa. Its ports gave it a role in Mediterranean trade, while monasteries such as Drazark preserved Armenian learning.
armenian-principality-of-cilicia.e: Byzantium temporarily regained Cilicia and imprisoned Leo I in 1137, but Thoros II restored the principality. In 1198 Leo II was crowned king with the blessing of the Holy Roman Emperor and the pope, transforming it into a kingdom.

arverni.t: Leading people of central Gaul, rulers of the Auvergne, whose noble Vercingetorix united Gaul against Caesar in 52 BCE.
arverni.o: The Arverni held the volcanic uplands and the fertile Limagne plain of the Auvergne. By the 2nd century BCE they dominated much of southern and central Gaul. Their king Luernios was remembered by Greek writers for scattering gold and silver to his followers, and his son Bituitus led a vast army against Rome.
arverni.r: Their power rested on a network of client peoples, such as the Gabali, Vellavi and Cadurci, and on great oppida like Corent and Gergovia, which imported Italian wine on a huge scale. After the defeat of Bituitus kingship was abolished, and Celtillus, father of Vercingetorix, was put to death for seeking to restore it.
arverni.e: Bituitus was defeated by the Roman Republic in 121 BCE. In 52 BCE Vercingetorix raised Gaul in revolt and repulsed Caesar at Gergovia, but surrendered at Alesia and was later executed in Rome. The Arverni were treated leniently, and their Roman capital Augustonemetum grew into Clermont-Ferrand.

ayyubid-emirate-of-kerak.t: An Ayyubid principality based on the Crusader castle of Kerak, which outlived the rest of Ayyubid Syria by three years.
ayyubid-emirate-of-kerak.o: Al-Nasir Dawud, son of al-Mu'azzam Isa of Damascus, lost Damascus to his uncles in 1229 but kept Kerak and the lands east of the Dead Sea, which became a separate principality.
ayyubid-emirate-of-kerak.r: Al-Nasir Dawud was a poet and scholar who used Kerak as a base for intrigue, briefly occupying Jerusalem in 1239 and sheltering the future sultan al-Salih Ayyub. The principality controlled the routes from Syria to Egypt and the Hijaz, and the near-impregnable castle made it a refuge. From 1250 al-Mughith Umar ruled Kerak, harbouring Mamluk dissidents and challenging the new regime in Egypt.
ayyubid-emirate-of-kerak.e: In 1263 the Mamluk sultan Baybars lured al-Mughith Umar out of Kerak, arrested and executed him, and annexed the principality.

ambracia.t: Corinthian colony in north-west Greece that became the capital of King Pyrrhus and was besieged and plundered by Rome in 189 BCE.
ambracia.o: Ambracia was founded c. 625 BCE by Corinthians under Gorgus, a son of the tyrant Cypselus, on the Arachthos river north of the Ambracian Gulf. It controlled fertile land and routes into Epirus, and Cypselid relatives ruled it as tyrants until the late 6th century BCE.
ambracia.r: Ambracia was a loyal ally of Corinth and Sparta. In the Peloponnesian War it fought the Acarnanians and Amphilochian Argos, and in 426 BCE the Athenian general Demosthenes destroyed its army at Idomene. It traded timber and goods with Epirus. Pyrrhus of the Kingdom of Epirus made it his capital and adorned it with palaces and statues.
ambracia.e: After joining the Aetolian League, Ambracia was besieged by Marcus Fulvius Nobilior in 189 BCE, who carried its works of art to Rome. It declined, and Augustus moved its people to Nicopolis. Modern Arta stands on the site.

alans.t: Iranian-speaking horse nomads of the North Caucasus steppe who raided Rome and Persia, followed the Vandals to Africa, and gave rise to the Ossetians.
alans.o: The Alans emerged in the 1st century CE among the Sarmatians on the steppes north of the Caucasus. Roman writers record their raids through the Caucasus passes into Armenia and Media in the 70s CE, and in the 130s the governor Arrian wrote a battle plan against them.
alans.r: They lived as mounted herders in clans under chiefs, moving with wagons and fighting as heavy cavalry with lances, a style that influenced Roman cavalry. Ammianus Marcellinus described their worship of a naked sword. They traded and fought with the Roman Empire, the Parthian Empire and the peoples of the steppe.
alans.e: The Hunnic Empire shattered them around 370. Some Alans moved west with the Vandals into Gaul, Spain and North Africa, while others stayed in the Caucasus foothills, became tributary to the Khazar Khaganate and formed the Kingdom of Alania. The Ossetians descend from them.

aden-settlement.t: Aden as a dependency of British India, seized in 1839 to serve as a coaling station on the steamship route to Bombay.
aden-settlement.o: In January 1839 forces of the British East India Company under Captain Stafford Haines captured Aden from the Sultanate of Lahej after a dispute over a plundered ship. Britain wanted a coaling station for steamships between Suez and Bombay, and Aden was governed from the Bombay Presidency.
aden-settlement.r: Haines served as political agent and built up the port, which had shrunk to a village. Aden was declared a free port in 1850, and after the Suez Canal opened in 1869 it became one of the world's busiest bunkering stations, with Indian, Somali, Jewish and Yemeni communities. From the 1870s Britain signed protection treaties with the hinterland rulers, creating the Aden Protectorate. Its administration passed to British India and then the British Raj.
aden-settlement.e: Under the Government of India Act of 1935, Aden was separated from India and became a Crown colony on 1 April 1937, as the Colony of Aden.
aden-settlement.re: Islam, with Hindu, Jewish and Christian minorities

aram-maacah.t: Aram-Maacah, a small Aramaean kingdom near Mount Hermon, known only from the Hebrew Bible.
aram-maacah.o: Maacah lay in the northern Golan and the slopes of Mount Hermon, north of Geshur. It is known only from the Hebrew Bible, which lists it among the Aramaean kingdoms of the 10th century BCE.
aram-maacah.r: Nothing is known of its government. The Bible relates that its king sent a thousand men to support Ammon against David of the United Kingdom of Israel.
aram-maacah.e: Maacah was absorbed by Aram-Damascus or the Kingdom of Israel in the 9th century BCE; the town of Abel-beth-maacah preserves its name.

arwad.t: Arwad, a tiny Phoenician island city off the Syrian coast whose sailors made it a naval power for more than a thousand years.
arwad.o: Arwad occupies a small island off Tartus, giving it a sheltered harbour and natural defences. A Canaanite town by the Late Bronze Age, it appears in the Amarna letters, and after 1200 BCE it became the northernmost of the great Phoenician cities, controlling the facing coast.
arwad.r: Kings ruled with a council of elders over a city of tall houses and a fleet of merchant ships. Arwad supplied ships to Tiglath-Pileser I of the Assyrian Empire, and its king Mattan-Baal sent troops to the coalition against Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BCE. It later contributed ships to the Persian fleet.
arwad.e: Arwad submitted to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 332 BCE, kept wide autonomy under the Seleucid Empire, and counted its own era from 259 BCE. It lost independence when Pompey annexed Syria in 64 BCE.

aegium.t: Achaean city on the Gulf of Corinth where the assembly of the Achaean League met at the sanctuary of Zeus Homarios.
aegium.o: Aegium lay on the southern shore of the Gulf of Corinth, one of the twelve Achaean cities of the northern Peloponnese. It grew in the early Iron Age on a terrace above a harbour; myth said Agamemnon gathered the Greek chiefs there before Troy.
aegium.r: The sanctuary of Zeus Homarios near Aegium was the religious centre of the Achaeans. After the Achaean League was refounded in 280 BCE, Aegium expelled its Macedonian garrison in 275 BCE and joined; the league's regular assemblies met there. The town lived from farming and the coastal trade of the gulf.
aegium.e: Philopoemen moved the meetings in rotation among member cities in the 180s BCE, reducing Aegium's role. It passed under Roman control in 146 BCE and continues as the modern town of Aigio.
aegium.re: Greek religion; cult of Zeus Homarios

avar-khanate.t: The leading Avar state of mountainous Dagestan for six centuries, centred on Khunzakh, whose khans were courted by Persia, the Ottomans and Russia.
avar-khanate.o: After the decline of Christian Sarir, a ruling house of Avar nutsals emerged at Khunzakh around the 12th and 13th centuries. Islam spread into the region during the 13th to 15th centuries, and the nutsals came to rule as Muslim khans over the Avar communities of the highlands.
avar-khanate.r: The khans held direct power over Khunzakh and nearby villages but relied on alliances with the self-governing Avar free communities, which had their own assemblies and customary law. Wealth came from herding, terraced farming and raiding. Umma Khan, who ruled from 1774, led raids deep into Georgia and Shirvan, and the khanate received subsidies from the Safavid Empire and later Russia.
avar-khanate.e: In 1834 the Caucasian Imamate's leader Hamzat Bek massacred the khan's family at Khunzakh, and the khanate was occupied by Shamil's forces. Restored under Russian protection after 1859, it was abolished by the Russian Empire in 1864 and turned into the Avar district.

austrasia.t: Eastern kingdom of the Merovingian Franks, centred on Metz and Reims, and the homeland of the Carolingian dynasty.
austrasia.o: Austrasia, the eastern land, arose from the share of Clovis' eldest son Theuderic I in 511, ruled from Reims and later Metz. It covered north-eastern France, the Rhineland, Belgium and the Netherlands, and was extended over Thuringia, Alemannia and Bavaria.
austrasia.r: Its population was more Germanic than that of Neustria, and its aristocracy was powerful. Sigebert I and his Visigothic queen Brunhild fought a long feud with Neustria. From the 7th century the mayors of the palace, above all the Pippinid family, held real power while kings reigned as figureheads.
austrasia.e: Pippin of Herstal defeated Neustria at Tertry in 687 and became master of the whole Kingdom of the Franks. His son Charles Martel and grandson Pippin the Short followed, and in 751 Pippin made himself king, ending Austrasia as a separate kingdom.

antanosy-kingdom.t: The kingdom of the Anosy region in south-east Madagascar, the first Malagasy state to confront a French colony on the island.
antanosy-kingdom.o: The Antanosy kingdom took shape around 1500 in the fertile Anosy region near modern Taolagnaro, under the Zafiraminia, a ruling clan claiming descent from Muslim immigrants. They kept Arabic-script writing and certain Islamic customs while ruling a largely Malagasy population.
antanosy-kingdom.r: Zafiraminia nobles held ritual privileges, including the exclusive right to slaughter cattle, and ruled over clans of commoners and slaves. The French governor Etienne de Flacourt described Antanosy society in detail in his History of the Great Island of Madagascar of 1658. Relations with the Fort-Dauphin Colony swung between trade and war, with the French seizing cattle and rice.
antanosy-kingdom.e: The French abandoned Fort-Dauphin in 1674 after an Antanosy uprising. The region remained divided among rival lords until the Merina Kingdom conquered it in 1825. The Antanosy remain a distinct people of south-east Madagascar.
antanosy-kingdom.re: Traditional Malagasy religion with Islamic elements

antemoro-kingdom.t: A south-east Malagasy kingdom of Islamic-influenced clans whose scribes kept the sorabe, Malagasy texts written in Arabic script.
antemoro-kingdom.o: The Antemoro formed around the Matitana river near Vohipeno in south-east Madagascar, where clans claiming descent from Muslim immigrants established a ruling aristocracy around 1500. Their traditions trace the founders to Mecca, though the migrants probably came via the Swahili coast or the Comoros.
antemoro-kingdom.r: Power lay with the Anteony noble clans, while scribal and priestly clans, the Anakara, guarded the sorabe manuscripts on astrology, medicine, history and divination. Antemoro diviners (ombiasy) became sought after as advisers at other Malagasy courts, including the Merina Kingdom. Society was rigidly stratified, and the kingdom produced distinctive paper made from bark.
antemoro-kingdom.e: Internal revolts in the 17th century weakened the noble clans, and in the 19th century the region fell under the Merina Kingdom. French colonial rule followed in 1895–96. The Antemoro remain one of Madagascar's ethnic groups, still known for their sorabe and Antaimoro paper.
antemoro-kingdom.re: Traditional Malagasy religion with Islamic elements

atzele.t: Latgalian borderland in north-eastern Latvia, contested between the crusaders and the Rus' of Pskov in the early 13th century.
atzele.o: Atzele, called Adzele in Latvian and Ochela in Rus' sources, lay in the north-eastern corner of modern Latvia, around Alūksne. It was a Latgalian district bordering Estonian Ugandi and the lands of Pskov.
atzele.r: Its people farmed and lived in communities centred on hillforts. The district was part of the Rus' tribute zone, and Pskov and Novgorod sent expeditions through it. Little is recorded of its rulers.
atzele.e: After the Livonian crusaders conquered neighbouring lands, Atzele was divided in 1224 between the bishop of Riga and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword and became part of Terra Mariana. Alūksne castle was later built in the area by the Livonian Order.

ayyubid-emirate-of-baalbek.t: An Ayyubid principality in the Beqaa Valley, held for half a century by the poet-prince al-Amjad Bahramshah.
ayyubid-emirate-of-baalbek.o: Saladin took Baalbek in 1174 and granted it in 1179 to his nephew Farrukh Shah. On Farrukh Shah's death in 1182 the town passed to his son al-Amjad Bahramshah.
ayyubid-emirate-of-baalbek.r: Baalbek's rulers lived within the great Roman temple complex, which had been turned into a citadel. Bahramshah ruled for nearly fifty years as a minor member of the Ayyubid family, depending on the stronger princes of Damascus, and was known as a poet. The district produced grain and fruit in the Beqaa and controlled the road from Damascus to Homs.
ayyubid-emirate-of-baalbek.e: Al-Ashraf Musa took Baalbek from Bahramshah in 1230, and it passed to al-Salih Ismail. The Mongols occupied the town in 1260 and damaged the citadel, and after Ain Jalut it came under the Mamluks.

ausci.t: Aquitanian people of Gascony whose chief town Elimberris became Auch, later the religious capital of the region.
ausci.o: The Ausci lived in the hills of central Gascony, in the modern Gers. They were among the Aquitani, whose language was related to Basque; the name of their town, Elimberris, is usually read as Basque-like 'new town', comparable with Iliberris in Iberia.
ausci.r: Pomponius Mela calls them the most distinguished of the Aquitanian peoples. Nothing is recorded of their rulers before the conquest.
ausci.e: The Ausci gave hostages to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE without fighting. Their town was refounded as Augusta Auscorum and in late antiquity became the metropolis of the province of Novempopulana. Auch remained the seat of an archbishop for all of Gascony.

aorsi.t: A powerful Sarmatian people between the Don and the Caspian, whose control of caravan routes made them rich in gold and allies of Rome.
aorsi.o: The Aorsi emerge in Greek sources in the 2nd century BCE as one of the leading Sarmatian groups, descended from the earlier steppe populations of the Sauromatae. Strabo divides them into a western group on the lower Don and the 'Upper Aorsi' further east, who ruled most of the Caspian shore.
aorsi.r: Strabo reports that the Aorsi could field 200,000 horsemen and that the Upper Aorsi wore gold because they carried Indian and Babylonian goods on camels from Armenia and Media. They were pastoral nomads organised under kings, and they appear in the politics of the Bosporan Kingdom, fighting with Rome against the Siraces in 49 CE under their king Eunones.
aorsi.e: From the late 1st century CE the Aorsi fade from the record as the Alans rose to dominate the same steppes. Most historians think they were absorbed into the Alan confederation, which the Huns overran in the 370s.

arretium.t: Northern Etruscan city, home of the bronze Chimera of Arezzo, which grew rich on farming and metalworking and became an early Roman ally.
arretium.o: Arretium, Etruscan Aritim, modern Arezzo, lay where the Val di Chiana meets the upper Arno, controlling routes between Etruria, Umbria and the Po valley. It developed into a city from the 6th century BCE, later than most Etruscan centres, and grew powerful in the 4th century BCE.
arretium.r: Arretium was known for agriculture and metalwork. The bronze Chimera of Arezzo, cast around 400 BCE and found in 1553, is a masterpiece of Etruscan art. The city was dominated by great families, among them the Cilnii, whom Livy reports being driven out by a popular revolt in 302 BCE and restored with Roman help; the Augustan minister Maecenas was descended from them.
arretium.e: Arretium made truces with Rome in 310 and 294 BCE and became a loyal ally, supplying weapons and grain to Scipio in 205 BCE. Under Rome it became famous for Arretine ware, a red-glazed tableware exported across the empire. The town continued as Arezzo, birthplace of Petrarch.

alash-autonomy.t: The Kazakh national government of the Alash party, which sought autonomy during the Russian Civil War and whose leaders were later killed in Stalin's purges.
alash-autonomy.o: The Alash party was founded by Kazakh intellectuals including Alikhan Bukeikhanov, Akhmet Baitursynov and Mirzhakip Dulatov. In December 1917 the Second All-Kazakh Congress in Orenburg proclaimed the Alash Autonomy and formed a government, the Alash Orda.
alash-autonomy.r: Alash Orda, led by Bukeikhanov, sought a Kazakh autonomy within a democratic Russian federation and governed from Semey (Semipalatinsk) with an eastern branch, while a western wing operated in Zhympity. It tried to build a militia and promoted Kazakh education and a reformed Arabic script. It allied with the Whites at times while negotiating with the Bolsheviks.
alash-autonomy.e: Disillusioned with the Whites, Alash leaders accepted Soviet power in 1919 and 1920, when the government was dissolved and the Kazakh lands became the Kirghiz, later Kazakh ASSR. Most of its leaders were executed in the purges of the 1930s; they were rehabilitated in the late Soviet period.

airenosi.t: A Pyrenean people known only from Polybius' list of those Hannibal conquered in 218 BCE, possibly of the Val d'Aran.
airenosi.o: The Airenosi appear in Polybius among the peoples between the Ebro and the Pyrenees subdued by Hannibal in 218 BCE. Their location is uncertain; they are often placed in the central Pyrenees, perhaps in the Val d'Aran, on the basis of their name.
airenosi.r: Nothing is known of their society or government.
airenosi.e: After Hannibal's conquest the region was held for Carthage by Hanno until the Roman advance. It came under Rome in the early 2nd century BCE, and the Airenosi disappear from the record.

ashnakkum.t: Ashnakkum, a kingdom of the upper Khabur region in the age of Mari, one of the shifting players in the politics of northern Mesopotamia.
ashnakkum.o: Ashnakkum was a city of the Ida-Maras district in north-eastern Syria, often identified with Chagar Bazar, though this is debated. Chagar Bazar, excavated by Max Mallowan in the 1930s, served as a provincial centre under Shamshi-Adad's Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia in the early 18th century BCE.
ashnakkum.r: After Shamshi-Adad's death Ashnakkum became an independent kingdom that appears often in the Mari letters, alternately allied with and opposed to Zimri-Lim. Tablets from Chagar Bazar record rations and administration of farmland, livestock and workers.
ashnakkum.e: Ashnakkum fell under the shadow of Babylon after the destruction of Mari c. 1760 BCE and lost its independence. The region later formed part of the Mitanni Empire.

artuqids-of-hasankeyf.t: A Turkmen dynasty on the Tigris that ruled Hasankeyf and Amid and employed the engineer al-Jazari, author of a celebrated book of machines.
artuqids-of-hasankeyf.o: The Artuqids descended from Artuq, a Turkmen commander of the Seljuks. His son Sokmen, who lost Jerusalem to the Fatimids in 1098, took Hisn Kayfa (Hasankeyf) on the Tigris in 1102 and helped defeat the Crusaders at Harran in 1104.
artuqids-of-hasankeyf.r: The Hasankeyf line ruled the upper Tigris valley and from 1183, when Saladin gave them Amid, the city of Diyarbakir. They built the great bridge at Hasankeyf and repaired the walls of Amid. At their court Ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari completed around 1206 his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, describing water clocks, automata and pumps. Their coins often carried figurative images borrowed from Byzantine and classical models.
artuqids-of-hasankeyf.e: Caught between the Ayyubids and the Sultanate of Rum, the dynasty lost Hasankeyf and Amid to the Ayyubid al-Kamil in 1232, and the Ayyubids of Hisn Kayfa took over.

angrivarii.t: A Germanic people of the middle Weser whose earthen boundary wall became the site of a major battle between Germanicus and Arminius in 16 CE.
angrivarii.o: The Angrivarii lived on both banks of the middle Weser, north of the Cherusci, in what is now Lower Saxony and eastern Westphalia. They appear in Roman sources around the time of Drusus' campaigns, and were at times allies, at times enemies of Rome.
angrivarii.r: Little is known of their government. Tacitus mentions a broad earthwork they had built to mark their boundary with the Cherusci; in 16 CE Germanicus fought the Battle of the Angrivarian Wall there after his victory at Idistaviso. After a revolt against Rome they submitted and returned Roman captives bought from other tribes.
angrivarii.e: Around 98 Tacitus reports that the Angrivarii and Chamavi had moved into the lands of the defeated Bructeri. They were later absorbed into the Saxons; their name survives in Engern (Angria), one of the three provinces of Old Saxony, alongside Westphalia and Eastphalia.

aden-protectorate.t: Britain's patchwork of some two dozen protected sultanates, emirates and sheikhdoms in the hinterland of Aden, the core of later South Yemen.
aden-protectorate.o: To secure the Aden Settlement and keep the Ottoman Empire away from it, Britain signed treaties with the tribal rulers around Aden from the 1870s, beginning with the Sultanate of Lahej and its neighbours, and later with the Hadrami states. Each ruler gave Britain control of his foreign relations in return for protection and stipends.
aden-protectorate.r: Britain at first intervened little in internal affairs. From 1937 the territory was divided into a Western and an Eastern Aden Protectorate, with political officers and local forces such as the Aden Protectorate Levies. In Hadramawt the agent Harold Ingrams negotiated a truce among hundreds of feuding tribes in 1937, known as Ingrams' Peace. An Anglo-Ottoman line of 1904-1914 marked the border with Yemen.
aden-protectorate.e: In 1959 most western states formed the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South, later the Federation of South Arabia; the eastern states, including the Qu'aiti Sultanate, remained outside. All were swept away by the National Liberation Front in 1967 and absorbed into South Yemen.

assuwa.t: Assuwa, a short-lived league of western Anatolian lands that rose against the Hittites c. 1430 BCE and may have given Asia its name.
assuwa.o: Assuwa was a coalition of 22 lands in north-western Anatolia, including Wilusiya and Taruisa, often linked with Troy. It formed in the 15th century BCE in resistance to Hittite expansion westward.
assuwa.r: Known almost only from the annals of Tudhaliya I of the Hittite Empire, the league was led by Piyama-Kurunta and his son Kukkuli. A bronze sword of Aegean type, inscribed with Tudhaliya's dedication after the victory over Assuwa, was found at Hattusa in 1991.
assuwa.e: Tudhaliya I defeated the coalition and deported thousands of soldiers and chariots. Kukkuli rebelled again and was killed. The name may survive in the Greek and Roman name Asia.

arzawa.t: Arzawa, the main kingdom of western Anatolia in the Late Bronze Age, a rival of the Hittites courted by Egypt.
arzawa.o: Arzawa emerged by the 16th century BCE in western Anatolia, with its capital at Apasa, later Ephesus. Its Luwian-speaking rulers dominated the river valleys of the Aegean hinterland and exploited every period of Hittite weakness to expand eastward.
arzawa.r: In the 14th century BCE Arzawa was strong enough for Amenhotep III of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom to negotiate a marriage with the daughter of King Tarhundaradu; the two Amarna letters involved are written in Hittite. The kingdom had links with the Mycenaean Ahhiyawa across the Aegean.
arzawa.e: Mursili II of the Hittite Empire defeated King Uhha-ziti c. 1320 BCE and took Apasa; Uhha-ziti fled to the islands of Ahhiyawa. The Hittites divided Arzawa into vassal states, including Mira, the Seha River Land and Hapalla.

aequi.t: Mountain people east of Rome whose raids threatened Latium in the 5th century BCE, the enemies defeated by the legendary Cincinnatus.
aequi.o: The Aequi lived in the upper valleys of the Aniene, Turano and Salto rivers in the Apennines east of Latium. They were probably a Sabellic people, though their language is unknown. They appear in Roman history in the early 5th century BCE, pushing into the Latin plain through the pass of Mount Algidus.
aequi.r: Known only from Roman sources, the Aequi lived in small fortified hill settlements and raided the farmland of Latium, often in alliance with the Volsci. Their most famous episode is Cincinnatus's rescue of a trapped Roman army at Mount Algidus in 458 BCE.
aequi.e: Rome gradually drove them back. In 304 BCE, Livy says, Rome captured 31 of their towns in 50 days and almost wiped out the people. Roman colonies were planted at Alba Fucens in 303 BCE and Carseoli in 298 BCE, and surviving Aequian communities became Roman.

austrian-empire.t: The Habsburg monarchy as a hereditary empire, the conservative pillar of Metternich's Europe from Napoleon to the Compromise with Hungary.
austrian-empire.o: Facing Napoleon's proclamation as Emperor of the French, Francis II proclaimed the Austrian Empire in August 1804, uniting the Habsburg hereditary lands, Bohemia and Hungary under one imperial title. When he dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, he continued as Francis I of Austria.
austrian-empire.r: Under Chancellor Metternich, Austria led the Congress of Vienna and presided over the German Confederation, suppressing liberal and national movements through censorship and police. The empire was multinational, with Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Italians and others, and Catholic in its institutions. The revolutions of 1848 were crushed with Russian help, and the young Franz Joseph ruled through centralised neo-absolutism in the 1850s.
austrian-empire.e: Defeats at Solferino in 1859 and Königgrätz in 1866 cost Austria Lombardy, Venetia and its leadership in Germany. The Compromise of 1867 with Hungary transformed the empire into the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary.

aulerci-diablintes.t: Branch of the Aulerci in the western Mayenne whose Roman town at Jublains preserves one of the best surviving Roman forts in France.
aulerci-diablintes.o: The Aulerci were a group of related peoples in north-western Gaul; the Diablintes held the area around Jublains in Mayenne, between the Cenomani and the Redones. Caesar names them among the allies of the Veneti, and Ptolemy gives their town as Noviodunum.
aulerci-diablintes.r: Very little is known of their society before the conquest. They shared in the Atlantic and Armorican trade networks and struck coins of Armorican type.
aulerci-diablintes.e: After joining the Veneti in 56 BCE they were defeated and absorbed into Gallia Lugdunensis. Their Roman town of Noviodunum Diablintum at Jublains, with its temple, baths, theatre and fortified store-building, declined in late antiquity when the civitas merged with that of the Cenomani.

austrian-netherlands.t: The southern Low Countries under Austrian Habsburg rule, a prosperous but contested land whose resistance to Joseph II's reforms foreshadowed Belgium.
austrian-netherlands.o: After the War of the Spanish Succession, the Treaties of Utrecht and Rastatt in 1713–1714 transferred the Spanish Netherlands to Emperor Charles VI. The Barrier Treaty of 1715 allowed Dutch garrisons in a line of fortresses against France.
austrian-netherlands.r: Governors ruled from Brussels, the most popular being Charles of Lorraine (1744–1780). The Ostend Company, founded in 1722 to trade with Asia, was suppressed in 1731 under Dutch and British pressure. France occupied the country after Fontenoy in 1745–1748. Agriculture, roads and industry developed under Maria Theresa, and Brussels gained neoclassical squares.
austrian-netherlands.e: Joseph II's centralising and church reforms sparked the Brabant Revolution of 1789 and the short-lived United Belgian States. Austria restored control in 1790, but French victory at Fleurus in 1794 led to annexation in 1795, confirmed by the Treaty of Campo Formio in 1797.

abdallab-sheikhdom.t: The Arab sheikhdom of Qerri, partner of the Funj sultans, which governed the northern Sudanese Nile as their chief vassal for three centuries.
abdallab-sheikhdom.o: The Abdallab descended from Abdallah Jamma, leader of the Qawasma Arabs, who allied with the Funj leader Amara Dunqas to destroy Alodia around 1504. Abdallah established his seat at Qerri, north of the confluence of the Blue and White Niles, controlling the routes north toward Egypt.
abdallab-sheikhdom.r: The Abdallab chiefs, titled manjil, ruled the Arab tribes and the northern provinces as viceroys of the Funj Sultanate, collecting tribute and controlling trade with Egypt. Ajib al-Kafuta, the most famous chief, sought greater independence and was killed by the Funj around 1611; afterwards the sheikhs remained subordinate but influential.
abdallab-sheikhdom.e: The Abdallab lost much of their power in the 18th century as the Hamaj regents dominated Sennar. In 1821 they submitted to the invading army of Egypt under Muhammad Ali, and the Turco-Egyptian Sudan absorbed their lands.

aptera.t: Hilltop city above Souda Bay in western Crete, whose name myth linked to Sirens who lost their wings in a contest with the Muses.
aptera.o: Aptera stood on a plateau overlooking Souda Bay in western Crete. A place called a-pa-ta-wa in Linear B tablets from Knossos may be its forerunner. The city grew in the Archaic period; its name, meaning wingless, was explained by a legend that the Sirens lost their feathers after losing a singing contest to the Muses.
aptera.r: Aptera had a port at Kisamos on Souda Bay and walls nearly four kilometres long. Like other Cretan cities it supplied mercenaries to Hellenistic kings, and its coins show Artemis and the hero Apteros. Inscriptions record treaties with Teos and other Greek states.
aptera.e: Aptera came under Rome in the conquest of 69 to 67 BCE and prospered as a Roman town, with large cisterns. It was largely abandoned after an earthquake in the 7th century CE.

anglo-corsican-kingdom.t: A two-year union of Corsica with the British crown, created by Pasquale Paoli to escape revolutionary France.
anglo-corsican-kingdom.o: Pasquale Paoli returned to Corsica in 1790 but broke with the French Revolution. In 1794, with British naval help, Corsican forces drove the French from the island; Nelson lost the sight of an eye at the siege of Calvi. A Corsican assembly at Corte voted to offer the crown to George III.
anglo-corsican-kingdom.r: The kingdom had a liberal constitution with an elected parliament, under a British viceroy, Sir Gilbert Elliot, who governed from Bastia. Paoli expected to lead the government but was sidelined and left for London in 1795. Britain valued the island as a naval base in the Mediterranean.
anglo-corsican-kingdom.e: Napoleon's victories in Italy in 1796 made the island hard to hold, and Spain's alliance with France threatened British naval control. The British evacuated Corsica in October 1796, and it returned to the French First Republic.

athens.t: The city-state of Attica that created democracy, led the Delian League and produced the drama, philosophy and architecture at the heart of Classical Greek culture.
athens.o: Athens was inhabited continuously from the Bronze Age, and the Acropolis held a Mycenaean palace. In the early Iron Age the communities of Attica were unified under Athens, a process the Greeks credited to Theseus. Kings gave way to annual archons drawn from the aristocracy, and the city adopted Draco's written laws in 621 BCE.
athens.r: Solon's reforms of 594 BCE ended debt bondage; Peisistratus then ruled as tyrant, and Cleisthenes founded democracy in 508 BCE. Athens defeated Persia at Marathon and Salamis, then led the Delian League. Under Pericles it built the Parthenon and staged the plays of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, funded by silver from Laurion.
athens.e: Defeat by Sparta in 404 BCE ended its empire, though it led the Second Athenian League until Chaeronea in 338 BCE. Under Macedonian and Roman influence it remained a centre of philosophy. After it sided with Mithridates, Sulla sacked Athens in 86 BCE.

amphictyonic-league.t: Ancient religious association of Greek peoples that managed the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi and repeatedly declared sacred wars that drew in the great powers.
amphictyonic-league.o: An amphictyony was a league of neighbours sharing a sanctuary. This one began at the shrine of Demeter at Anthela near Thermopylae and extended its care to Delphi. Its role became prominent in the First Sacred War, traditionally c. 595-585 BCE, when members destroyed the town of Kirrha for abusing pilgrims and then reorganised the Pythian Games in 582 BCE.
amphictyonic-league.r: Twelve peoples, among them the Thessalians, Phocians, Boeotians, Dorians and Ionians, each sent two delegates (hieromnemones) to a council meeting twice a year at Anthela and Delphi. The council looked after temple property and finances, the Pythian Games and the sacred land, and could fine or declare war on offenders. Powerful states used its votes to dress political aims as piety.
amphictyonic-league.e: The Third Sacred War against Phocis (356-346 BCE) brought Philip II of Macedon onto the council, and the Fourth (339 BCE) led to his victory at Chaeronea. The Aetolian League dominated it in the 3rd century BCE. Augustus reorganised its membership, and it lingered as a religious body into the 2nd century CE.
amphictyonic-league.re: Ancient Greek religion (cult of Apollo and Demeter)

achaean-league.t: Federation of Peloponnesian cities that grew under Aratus and Philopoemen to unite the whole Peloponnese before its destruction by Rome in 146 BCE.
achaean-league.o: An older league of the small cities of Achaea on the Gulf of Corinth had collapsed under Macedonian rule. In 280 BCE four cities, Dyme, Patrae, Tritaia and Pharai, refounded it. Aratus brought in Sicyon in 251 BCE and seized Acrocorinth from the Macedonians in 243 BCE, making the league a major power.
achaean-league.r: Members kept local government but shared citizenship, coinage, weights and foreign policy. Assemblies met at Aigion, electing an annual general (strategos), who could not serve consecutive terms. Polybius, himself an Achaean, praised it as a model of federal union. Under Philopoemen it absorbed Sparta, Messene and Elis, uniting the Peloponnese by 191 BCE.
achaean-league.e: War with Cleomenes III forced Aratus to invite back Macedon. Rome later used disputes over Sparta to intervene; in 146 BCE the league declared war, and Lucius Mummius destroyed Corinth. The league was dissolved, revived later only as a minor body.

abydos.t: Milesian colony at the narrowest point of the Hellespont, where Xerxes bridged the strait and where legend placed the love of Hero and Leander.
abydos.o: Settlers from Miletus founded Abydos c. 680 BCE on the Asian shore of the Hellespont, at the narrows opposite Sestos, with the agreement of the Lydian king Gyges. Its position controlled the crossing between Europe and Asia and the passage of ships to the Black Sea.
abydos.r: Abydos lived from trade and fishing. In 480 BCE Xerxes built his boat bridges across the strait near the city. It joined the Delian League but revolted in 411 BCE, becoming a Spartan base, and the Battle of Abydos was fought off its shore that year. Greek legend set the story of Leander, who swam to Hero at Sestos, here.
abydos.e: In 200 BCE Philip V of the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia besieged Abydos; rather than surrender, many citizens killed their families and themselves. Rome later freed it, and it joined the province of Asia in 129 BCE.

ancient-veneti.t: Iron Age people of north-eastern Italy, centred on Ateste and Patavium, famed for horse-breeding and bronze work, who became Rome's peaceful allies and gave their name to Venice.
ancient-veneti.o: The Veneti emerged in the plain between the Po, the Adige and the Alps in the early 1st millennium BCE, forming the Este culture from about 1000 BCE. Greek and Roman writers linked them to the Eneti of Paphlagonia or to Trojan refugees under Antenor, legends Padua later embraced, but archaeology shows a mainly local development.
ancient-veneti.r: Their main centres were Ateste (Este), Patavium (Padua), Vicetia and Altinum, each probably self-governing. They wrote Venetic, an Indo-European language, in an alphabet adapted from Etruscan, known from hundreds of votive inscriptions. Bronze situlae decorated with processions and banquets, amber trade from the Baltic, and celebrated horse-breeding marked their culture; the healing goddess Reitia had a major sanctuary at Este.
ancient-veneti.e: Hostile to the Gauls, the Veneti allied with Rome from the 3rd century BCE and were absorbed gradually and without conquest. Latin replaced Venetic, and Caesar's grant of citizenship in 49 BCE completed integration. Their name lived on in the Roman region of Venetia et Histria and, through it, in Venice and the Veneto.
