antipatrid-kingdom-of-macedonia.t: Macedon under Cassander, son of Antipater, who ended Alexander the Great's line, founded Thessalonica and briefly passed the throne to his sons.
antipatrid-kingdom-of-macedonia.o: After the regent Antipater died in 319 BCE, his son Cassander fought Polyperchon and Olympias for Macedon and won control by 316 BCE, executing Olympias. He married Alexander's half-sister Thessalonike. Around 310 BCE he had Alexander IV and his mother Roxane killed, and in 305 BCE took the title of king.
antipatrid-kingdom-of-macedonia.r: Cassander ruled from Pella with the support of the Macedonian aristocracy, controlling much of Greece through garrisons and friendly governments, such as that of Demetrius of Phalerum at Athens. He refounded Thebes and founded Thessalonica and Cassandreia, the latter on the site of Potidaea. He was an ally of Lysimachus, Seleucus and Ptolemy against Antigonus I.
antipatrid-kingdom-of-macedonia.e: Cassander died in 297 BCE. His son Philip IV died soon after, and the brothers Antipater II and Alexander V fought over the throne. Demetrius Poliorcetes, called in by Alexander V, murdered him in 294 BCE and took Macedon, ending the dynasty and opening the way for the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia.

audhali-sultanate.t: A highland sultanate north-east of Aden and a founding member of the British-backed Federation of Arab Emirates of the South.
audhali-sultanate.o: The Audhali tribe held the Kawr al-Awadhil plateau and the plain below it, north-east of Aden. Its sultans, based at Zara, emerged as an independent local power around 1800, after the authority of the Qasimid State in the south had faded.
audhali-sultanate.r: The sultanate was a tribal state with little formal administration, its people farming the high plateau and controlling routes from the coast inland. It entered British protection in the late 19th century as part of the Aden Protectorate. In 1959 it was one of the six founding members of the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South, and its rulers held posts in the federal government.
audhali-sultanate.e: After the Federation of South Arabia collapsed in 1967, the National Liberation Front took over the territory, abolished the sultanate and incorporated it into South Yemen.

arab-kingdom-of-syria.t: The first modern Arab state, proclaimed in Damascus under Faisal in 1920 and destroyed by France within months.
arab-kingdom-of-syria.o: Faisal, son of the Sharif of Mecca, entered Damascus in October 1918 with the Arab army of the revolt against the Ottomans and set up a government under the British-led Occupied Enemy Territory Administration. On 8 March 1920 the Syrian National Congress proclaimed him king of an independent Syria including Lebanon and Palestine.
arab-kingdom-of-syria.r: The government drew on Arab nationalist officers and notables, many of them former Ottoman officials. The Congress drafted a constitution for a constitutional monarchy, with Hashim al-Atassi as prime minister. The state's control was limited to the inland cities, and its finances depended on British subsidies that ended in 1919.
arab-kingdom-of-syria.e: The San Remo conference gave France the mandate for Syria in April 1920. France sent an ultimatum, and on 24 July 1920 its army defeated the Syrian force at Maysalun, where the war minister Yusuf al-Azma was killed. Faisal was expelled and became king of Iraq in 1921.

araucania.t: The lands of the Mapuche south of the Biobío river, which resisted Spanish conquest for three centuries and kept their independence until the 1880s.
araucania.o: When Pedro de Valdivia advanced south from Santiago in 1550, the Mapuche of the region between the Biobío and Toltén rivers rose against him. Under leaders such as Lautaro and Caupolicán they defeated and killed Valdivia at Tucapel in 1553, beginning the long Arauco War.
araucania.r: The Mapuche had no central state. Each lineage was led by a lonko, and groups united under war leaders called toqui in times of conflict. After the victory at Curalaba in 1598, Mapuche forces destroyed the Spanish towns south of the Biobío. At the Parliament of Quillín in 1641 Spain recognised the river as the frontier, and later parlamentos regulated trade and peace. The Mapuche adopted horses and cattle and traded across the Andes into the pampas.
araucania.e: Independent Chile carried out the Occupation of Araucanía from 1861 to 1883, while Argentina's Conquest of the Desert subdued the Mapuche east of the Andes. Mapuche lands were confiscated and confined to reservations, and land claims remain a major political issue.

ayyubid-yemen.t: Yemen as a dominion of Saladin's family, which ended its many local dynasties and made Ta'izz a royal centre.
ayyubid-yemen.o: In 1174 Saladin sent his brother Turan-Shah with an army to Yemen. He defeated the Mahdid dynasty at Zabid, took Aden from the Zurayid dynasty and pressed the Hamdanid sultanate of Yemen, uniting the lowlands and much of the south under the Ayyubid Empire.
ayyubid-yemen.r: Yemen was ruled by Ayyubid princes as a valuable dependency, profiting from Aden's customs and the Red Sea trade. Tughtakin ibn Ayyub, ruler from 1182 to 1197, consolidated control, took Sanaa and made Ta'izz an important base. The Ayyubids promoted Sunni Islam, founded madrasas and introduced Kurdish and Turkic troops. The Zaydi imams resisted in the northern highlands.
ayyubid-yemen.e: In 1229 the last Ayyubid ruler, al-Mas'ud Yusuf, left for Egypt, appointing his commander Nur al-Din Umar ibn Rasul as deputy. Nur al-Din soon declared independence, founding the Rasulid dynasty.

auteini.t: People of western Ireland named by Ptolemy, usually placed in Galway or Mayo and possibly linked with the later Uaithni.
auteini.o: The Auteini, or Autini, are listed in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 on the west coast of Ireland, between the Nagnatae to the north and the Gangani (Ireland) to the south, roughly in modern Galway or Mayo. Ptolemy's Irish data came from earlier maritime reports and are imprecise.
auteini.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or society. Their name is often compared with the Uaithni, a population group recorded in early medieval Ireland in north Tipperary and Limerick, which could indicate a later movement south or a mistaken placing by Ptolemy, but the identification remains conjecture.
auteini.e: The Auteini do not appear in later records. The west of Ireland where Ptolemy placed them later formed part of the Kingdom of Connacht.

ayyubids-of-hisn-kayfa.t: The last surviving branch of the Ayyubid dynasty, ruling the Tigris town of Hasankeyf for nearly three centuries.
ayyubids-of-hisn-kayfa.o: In 1232 the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil took Hisn Kayfa and Amid from the Artuqids of Hasankeyf and gave them to his son al-Salih Ayyub. When al-Salih Ayyub went on to Egypt, a junior line of the family remained in Hasankeyf.
ayyubids-of-hisn-kayfa.r: Al-Salih Ayyub's son Turanshah left Hasankeyf in 1249 to take the throne in Egypt and was murdered by the Mamluks in 1250. The princes who stayed survived as vassals of the Mongols, the Ilkhanids, the Qara Qoyunlu and the Aq Qoyunlu. They built in Hasankeyf, including the El Rizk mosque of al-Adil Sulayman in 1409, and ruled a mixed Kurdish, Arab and Christian population.
ayyubids-of-hisn-kayfa.e: The dynasty was ended in the early 16th century as the Ottomans took over the region from the Safavids, its last princes being absorbed into the Ottoman system. Much of Hasankeyf was flooded by the Ilisu Dam in 2020.

a-group-chiefdom-of-qustul.t: An A-Group chiefdom in Lower Nubia whose rich royal tombs at Qustul rivalled those of predynastic Egypt.
a-group-chiefdom-of-qustul.o: The A-Group people lived in Lower Nubia, between the First and Second Cataracts, from about 3800 BCE. By c. 3300 BCE a ruling elite had emerged around Qustul, near the modern Egypt-Sudan border, growing rich as middlemen in the trade between Egypt and the south in ivory, ebony, incense and animal skins.
a-group-chiefdom-of-qustul.r: Cemetery L at Qustul contains large tombs with Egyptian stone vessels, imported pottery and gold. A carved incense burner shows a crowned figure resembling an Egyptian king, which led some scholars to argue that pharaonic kingship began here; most now see an elite sharing Upper Egyptian symbols. The A-Group made fine, thin-walled painted pottery and lived by herding, farming and trade.
a-group-chiefdom-of-qustul.e: Around 3000 to 2900 BCE the kings of Early Dynastic Egypt campaigned into Nubia, and a rock inscription at Gebel Sheikh Suleiman records an attack. The A-Group then disappears and Lower Nubia appears thinly settled until the C-Group arrived. Egyptians long called the region Ta-Seti, 'Land of the Bow'.

autonomous-republic-of-northern-epirus.t: Short-lived republic declared in 1914 by the Greek population of southern Albania, which won autonomy before the First World War overtook it.
autonomous-republic-of-northern-epirus.o: The Balkan Wars of 1912-1913 left Greek troops in southern Albania, a region with a large Greek Orthodox population that Greeks called Northern Epirus. The Protocol of Florence in December 1913 assigned it to the new state of Albania. Rejecting this, local leaders proclaimed an autonomous republic at Gjirokaster in February 1914, led by Georgios Christakis-Zografos.
autonomous-republic-of-northern-epirus.r: The provisional government raised its own armed units, issued stamps and fought Albanian gendarmerie for control of the region. In May 1914 the Protocol of Corfu, accepted by the Albanian government and the great powers, gave the region extensive autonomy within Albania, with Greek-language schools and Orthodox religious rights.
autonomous-republic-of-northern-epirus.e: The Protocol of Corfu was never fully put into effect. With the outbreak of the First World War and Albania's collapse, the Greek army occupied the region in October 1914, ending the republic. The area was returned to Albania after the war.

aydinids.t: An Aegean beylik whose fleets under Umur Bey raided the Greek world and provoked a crusade against Smyrna.
aydinids.o: Mehmed Bey, a commander in the service of the Germiyanids, conquered Birgi, Ayasoluk (Ephesus) and the upper Smyrna citadel from the Byzantines in the first decade of the 14th century and founded his own beylik, with Birgi as capital.
aydinids.r: Mehmed's son Umur Bey built a fleet at Smyrna and raided the Aegean islands, Greece and the Black Sea, and as an ally of John VI Kantakouzenos fought in the Byzantine civil war. In 1344 a crusading league took Smyrna's harbour castle, founding Crusader Smyrna, and Umur was killed trying to retake it in 1348. Ayasoluk prospered from Italian trade, and Isa Bey built the Isa Bey Mosque there in 1375.
aydinids.e: Bayezid I annexed the beylik in 1390, Timur restored it in 1402, and after the resistance of Cuneyd Bey the Ottomans took it finally in 1425-1426.

albici.t: Hardy mountain people of upper Provence who fought for Massalia against Caesar's siege in 49 BCE.
albici.o: The Albici lived in the hills north of Massalia, probably around the plateau of Albion and the area of Riez, whose Roman name Alebaece Reiorum may preserve theirs. Caesar describes them as old clients of Massalia.
albici.r: Caesar calls them barbarians living in the mountains above Massilia, under the protection of the Greek city, and praises their courage. No rulers or institutions are recorded.
albici.e: In 49 BCE the Massaliots brought the Albici into the city as defenders against Caesar's legates, but the siege ended in surrender. Their land was then absorbed into Gallia Narbonensis.

alchon-huns.t: A Hunnic people who ruled Kabulistan and Gandhara and invaded northern India, remembered in Indian tradition for the destructive kings Toramana and Mihirakula.
alchon-huns.o: The Alchon Huns emerged in Bactria in the late 4th century, probably among the Hunnic groups that followed the Chionites and Kidarites. They first issued coins copying the Sasanian king Shapur II, then moved south of the Hindu Kush, taking Kabul and later replacing the Kidarites in Gandhara in the mid-5th century.
alchon-huns.r: Known mainly from coins with their distinctive elongated skulls and the Bactrian word 'alchono', and from Indian inscriptions, they ruled as warrior kings over a settled population. Around 500 Toramana invaded the Gupta Empire, reaching central India, as recorded at Eran. His son Mihirakula ruled from Sakala and was remembered by Buddhist writers such as Xuanzang as a persecutor who destroyed monasteries.
alchon-huns.e: Mihirakula was defeated around 528 by the Indian king Yasodharman and possibly by the Guptas, and Alchon power retreated to Kashmir and Gandhara. By the mid-6th century their rule faded, and they were succeeded in the Kabul region by the Nezak Huns.

abydos-dynasty.t: A small, debated local dynasty at Abydos in the Second Intermediate Period, made real by the 2014 discovery of King Senebkay's tomb.
abydos-dynasty.o: In 1997 the Egyptologist Kim Ryholt proposed that a group of kings in the Turin King List ruled a local kingdom at Abydos around 1650 BCE, after the collapse of the Middle Kingdom of Egypt. The idea remains debated, but it was strengthened in 2014 when Josef Wegner's team found the tomb of a previously unknown king, Senebkay, at Abydos.
abydos-dynasty.r: Almost nothing is known of its government. The kings ruled a narrow stretch of Middle Egypt around Abydos and Thinis, the cult centre of Osiris. Senebkay's modest tomb reused materials from older monuments, and his skeleton bears battle wounds, perhaps from fighting the Hyksos.
abydos-dynasty.e: The kingdom probably fell by around 1600 BCE, absorbed by the Theban Sixteenth Dynasty of Egypt or overrun by the Hyksos.

artuqids-of-mardin.t: The longest-lived branch of the Artuqid dynasty, ruling the hilltop city of Mardin for three centuries under Seljuk, Ayyubid and Mongol overlords.
artuqids-of-mardin.o: Ilghazi, son of the Turkmen commander Artuq, took Mardin in the early 12th century and made it the base of his branch of the family. In 1118 he also gained Aleppo, and in 1119 he destroyed the army of the Principality of Antioch at the Field of Blood.
artuqids-of-mardin.r: His son Timurtash and later rulers held Mardin and Mayyafariqin, survived by accepting Zengid, Ayyubid and then Ilkhanid overlordship, and kept their dynasty intact through repeated invasions. Mardin, terraced on a steep hill, gained mosques and madrasas, notably the Sultan Isa or Zinciriye Madrasa of 1385. The region was home to many Syriac Christians, including the patriarchal monastery of Deyrulzafaran.
artuqids-of-mardin.e: Timur took Mardin's lower city in 1394 and 1401. The last Artuqids were displaced by the Qara Qoyunlu leader Qara Yusuf in 1409, and Mardin later passed to the Aq Qoyunlu and the Ottomans.

archduchy-of-austria.t: The Habsburg heartland on the Danube, raised to an archduchy in 1453, around which the dynasty built its great central European monarchy.
archduchy-of-austria.o: The Duchy of Austria had been held by the Habsburgs since 1278. Duke Rudolf IV forged the Privilegium Maius around 1358, claiming the title of archduke. In 1453 Emperor Frederick III, himself a Habsburg, confirmed the forgery, giving the rulers of Austria the rank of archduke and special privileges.
archduchy-of-austria.r: The archduchy, divided into Austria below and above the Enns, was governed from Vienna, where strong estates of nobles, clergy and towns met in diets. Its archdukes were usually also emperors. Much of the nobility turned Protestant in the 16th century but was forced back to Catholicism after 1620. Vienna withstood Ottoman sieges in 1529 and 1683.
archduchy-of-austria.e: From 1526 the archduchy formed the core of the Habsburg Monarchy. In 1804 Francis II proclaimed the Austrian Empire, in which the archduchy remained a crown land until 1918; its territory now forms the federal states of Lower Austria, Upper Austria and Vienna.

artuqids-of-harput.t: A branch of the Artuqid dynasty at the fortress of Harput, where Belek Ghazi held the King of Jerusalem captive.
artuqids-of-harput.o: Harput, a fortress near the upper Euphrates, came under Artuqid rule early in the 12th century. Its most famous holder was Belek Ghazi, a nephew of Ilghazi, who captured Joscelin I of the County of Edessa in 1122 and King Baldwin II of Jerusalem in 1123 and imprisoned them there.
artuqids-of-harput.r: Armenian sympathisers briefly seized Harput castle to free the captives in 1123, but Belek retook it. He was killed besieging Manbij in 1124. Harput then belonged to the Artuqids of Hasankeyf until a separate line was established in 1185 by Imad al-Din Abu Bakr. The small emirate built mosques, notably the Ulu Cami of Harput.
artuqids-of-harput.e: Squeezed between the Ayyubids and the Sultanate of Rum, the Harput branch was annexed by the Seljuk sultan Kayqubad I in 1234.

angevin-empire.t: The vast assemblage of lands ruled by Henry II and his sons, from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees, which collapsed in the wars with Philip II.
angevin-empire.o: Henry II inherited Anjou, Maine and Touraine from his father Geoffrey Plantagenet and Normandy through his mother Matilda, gained Aquitaine by marrying Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1152, and became king of England in 1154. He also asserted lordship over Ireland from 1171 and over Brittany through his son Geoffrey.
angevin-empire.r: There was no single government: each land kept its own customs, though Henry built strong royal justice in England and moved constantly between his territories. Chinon was a favourite residence and treasury. Henry's sons rebelled repeatedly, backed by the French kings. Richard I spent most of his reign on crusade and in France, building Château Gaillard to guard Normandy.
angevin-empire.e: King John lost Normandy, Anjou and Maine to Philip II in 1202–1204, and his allies' defeat at Bouvines in 1214 ended hopes of recovery. England kept Gascony, and the term Angevin Empire was coined by modern historians.

armenian-kingdom-of-cilicia.t: An Armenian kingdom on the Mediterranean that allied with Crusaders and Mongols and was the last independent Armenian state of the Middle Ages.
armenian-kingdom-of-cilicia.o: Around 1080, as Byzantine rule in the East collapsed, the Armenian lord Ruben established himself in the Taurus mountains of Cilicia. His Rubenid descendants expanded into the Cilician plain, and in 1198 Leo I was crowned king with the blessing of the Holy Roman Emperor and the pope.
armenian-kingdom-of-cilicia.r: Cilicia combined Armenian traditions with Frankish feudal institutions, titles and law, and its nobles intermarried with Crusader families. The port of Ayas carried Venetian and Genoese trade in silk and spices. Hethum I submitted to the Mongols and travelled to Karakorum in 1254, allying with them against the Mamluks. The kingdom produced fine illuminated manuscripts, notably those of Toros Roslin, while the Catholicos resided at Sis and later Hromkla.
armenian-kingdom-of-cilicia.e: Repeated Mamluk invasions wore the kingdom down after Mongol power waned. In 1375 the Mamluks took Sis and captured Leo V of the Lusignan line, who died in exile in Paris in 1393. The title King of Armenia passed to the Lusignans of Cyprus.

ancalites.t: British people named once by Julius Caesar among those who surrendered to him in 54 BCE, leading him to the stronghold of Cassivellaunus.
ancalites.o: The Ancalites are known only from Caesar's Gallic War. In 54 BCE they were among five British peoples, alongside the Cenimagni, Segontiaci, Bibroci and Cassi, who sent embassies to submit after the Trinovantes had won his protection.
ancalites.r: Caesar says that from these envoys he learned the location of Cassivellaunus's stronghold, protected by woods and marshes, which he then stormed. Beyond this, nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs, and their territory is uncertain, though the upper Thames valley has been suggested.
ancalites.e: No later source mentions the Ancalites. They were probably absorbed by stronger neighbours such as the Catuvellauni or the Atrebates (Britain) in the century before the Roman conquest of 43.

albania.t: Present-day Albania, a parliamentary republic since the end of communism in 1991 and a NATO member seeking to join the European Union.
albania.o: Mass protests and emigration in 1990 forced the People's Socialist Republic of Albania to permit opposition parties. After the first multi-party elections, the country was renamed the Republic of Albania in April 1991. In 1992 the Democratic Party of Sali Berisha won power, ending communist rule.
albania.r: Albania is a parliamentary republic with a president elected by parliament. Religion returned to public life after decades of state atheism, and private enterprise and emigration transformed society. The collapse of pyramid investment schemes in 1997 caused near-anarchy and an international intervention. In 1999 Albania sheltered hundreds of thousands of refugees from Kosovo. Politics has been dominated by the rivalry of the Democratic and Socialist parties.
albania.e: Albania joined NATO in 2009, became an EU candidate in 2014 and opened accession negotiations in 2022. Edi Rama's Socialists have governed since 2013, and tourism has become a major industry.
albania.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

andorra.t: A Pyrenean co-principality created by a medieval agreement in 1278, still ruled jointly by the bishop of Urgell and the president of France.
andorra.o: Andorra's valleys had been held by the counts of Urgell and then the bishops of Urgell, whose rights were disputed by the counts of Foix. In 1278 Bishop Pere d'Urtx and Count Roger-Bernard III of Foix signed the first Pareatge, agreeing to share sovereignty, and a second agreement followed in 1288.
andorra.r: The co-princes ruled through local representatives, and the valleys governed themselves through parishes and, from 1419, the Consell de la Terra. Andorrans lived from herding, farming and smuggling, kept Catalan as their language and Catholicism as their faith, and avoided entanglement in the wars of their neighbours.
andorra.e: The Foix rights passed to the kings of Navarre and then the French crown, and so to the presidents of France. In the 20th century tourism and low taxes transformed the economy. A constitution in 1993 made Andorra a parliamentary co-principality, and it joined the United Nations that year.

autrigones.t: A people of northern Burgos and western Bizkaia, whose towns Virovesca and Flaviobriga linked the Meseta to the Cantabrian Sea.
autrigones.o: The Autrigones occupied the land from the upper Ebro to the coast around Castro Urdiales, in modern Burgos, Álava and Bizkaia, from the later Iron Age. They bordered the Cantabri, Turmodigi, Caristii and Berones, and their language was probably Celtic.
autrigones.r: They lived in hillforts and lowland settlements, farming and herding, with towns such as Virovesca (Briviesca) and Tritium Autrigonum named by Pliny and Ptolemy. Their political organisation is unknown.
autrigones.e: They came under Rome during the 1st century BCE, and after the Cantabrian Wars their territory became part of Hispania Tarraconensis. The Flavian emperors founded the port of Flaviobriga on their coast, modern Castro Urdiales.

avar-khaganate.t: Steppe empire centred on the Carpathian basin that dominated central Europe's Slavs, besieged Constantinople and lasted until Charlemagne broke it.
avar-khaganate.o: The Avars came from the Eurasian steppe and reached the Byzantine frontier in 558. In 567 their khagan Bayan I allied with the Lombards to destroy the Kingdom of the Gepids, and after the Lombards left for Italy in 568 the Avars took the whole Carpathian basin.
avar-khaganate.r: The khagan ruled a mounted warrior elite over Slavs, Gepids and others. Byzantine tribute in gold financed the state, and Avar raids reached Italy and Thuringia. In 626 they besieged Constantinople with Persian support and failed, and many Slav subjects broke away. Later Avar graves show cast bronze belt fittings with griffins and tendrils, and earthwork rings served as royal centres.
avar-khaganate.e: From 791 Charlemagne's Franks attacked; in 795–796 they seized the treasure of the Ring. Avar leaders accepted Christianity and Frankish overlordship, and the First Bulgarian Empire took the east. The last mention of Avars comes in 822, and their land later passed to the Hungarians.

ammon.t: Ammon, an Iron Age kingdom of the Jordanian plateau around Rabbah, modern Amman, whose name lives on in Jordan's capital.
ammon.o: The Ammonites formed a kingdom in the 10th century BCE or earlier, on the plateau around the upper Jabbok river, with its capital at Rabbah, the citadel of modern Amman. The Bible portrays King Nahash as an enemy of Saul.
ammon.r: Ammonite kings ruled a farming and herding land guarded by watchtowers, under the national god Milkom. Inscriptions such as the Amman Citadel inscription and the Tell Siran bottle, which names King Amminadab, show a language close to Hebrew. Ammon prospered as a loyal vassal of the Assyrian Empire.
ammon.e: Under the Chaldean Empire, King Baalis plotted against Babylonian rule in Judah. A Babylonian campaign in 582 BCE ended Ammon's independence, and the land became a province. Rabbah was refounded as Philadelphia by the Ptolemaic Empire.

amisos.t: Amisos, a Greek port on the central Black Sea coast, later a royal city of the Pontic kings and the ancestor of Samsun.
amisos.o: Greek colonists, traditionally from Miletus, founded Amisos in the 6th century BCE on a bay of the Black Sea between the mouths of the Halys and the Iris. The city traded with the interior of Anatolia and became one of the leading ports of the southern coast.
amisos.r: Amisos was a self-governing Greek city that received Athenian settlers in the 5th century BCE, when it was briefly renamed Peiraieus. It recognised Persian and then Hellenistic overlords while keeping its institutions, minting coins and exporting grain, timber and metals.
amisos.e: From the accession of Mithridates VI in 120 BCE Amisos was a royal city of the Kingdom of Pontus, adorned by the king. The Roman general Lucullus captured it in 71 BCE, and it later flourished as a free city under Rome.

argentine-confederation.t: The loose union of Argentine provinces dominated by Juan Manuel de Rosas, which gave Argentina its 1853 constitution before Buenos Aires reunited the nation.
argentine-confederation.o: The Federal Pact of 1831 between Buenos Aires, Santa Fe and Entre Ríos, later joined by the other provinces after the defeat of the Unitarian League, created the Argentine Confederation. There was no national government; the governor of Buenos Aires conducted foreign relations on behalf of the provinces.
argentine-confederation.r: Juan Manuel de Rosas, governor of Buenos Aires from 1829 to 1832 and from 1835 to 1852 with total public power, dominated the confederation. His police, the Mazorca, terrorised Unitarian opponents. He resisted an Anglo-French blockade of the River Plate from 1845 to 1850. After Justo José de Urquiza defeated him at Caseros in 1852, a congress adopted the Constitution of 1853, still in force, and the government sat at Paraná.
argentine-confederation.e: Buenos Aires rejected the constitution and formed the separate State of Buenos Aires. After Bartolomé Mitre's victory at Pavón in 1861, the nation reunited as the Argentine Republic. The Constitution of 1853 remains the basis of Argentina's present constitution.

alderney.t: The northernmost of the inhabited Channel Islands, a self-governing part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey with its own States and a long history as a fortress.
alderney.o: Alderney was part of the Duchy of Normandy and stayed loyal to the English crown when King John lost mainland Normandy to France in 1204. Like the other Channel Islands it remained a possession of the crown in its role as Duke of Normandy, never part of the Kingdom of England.
alderney.r: The island was governed under Norman customary law, and from 1584 to 1825 held by hereditary governors. The British built a chain of Victorian forts and the breakwater at Braye. During the German occupation of 1940 to 1945 the population was evacuated and the Nazis built labour camps there.
alderney.e: Alderney's residents returned in 1945. Since 1949 it has been part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey for some matters, while keeping its own elected States of Alderney, and remains a British Crown Dependency.

ausetani.t: An Iberian people of the plain of Vic in Catalonia, whose name survives in the later County of Osona.
ausetani.o: The Ausetani lived on the plain of Vic and the surrounding hills in central Catalonia from about the 5th century BCE. Their chief town was Ausa, on the site of modern Vic, and the fortified settlement of L'Esquerda lay nearby.
ausetani.r: Little is known of their institutions beyond Livy's narrative. They lived from farming and herding, and minted coins with the Iberian legend Ausesken. During the Second Punic War they sided with Carthage, and their leader Amusicus fled to Hasdrubal when the Romans besieged their town for thirty days.
ausetani.e: After further resistance during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE, they were absorbed into Hispania Citerior. Ausa became the Roman town of Ausa, later Vicus Ausonensis, and their name lived on in the medieval County of Osona.

allobroges.t: Powerful Gallic people between the Rhône and the Isère, conquered by Rome in 121 BCE, whose envoys exposed the Catilinarian conspiracy.
allobroges.o: The Allobroges held the land between the Rhône, the Isère and Lake Geneva, in the modern Isère and Savoy. Their chief town was Vienna (Vienne), and Genava (Geneva) stood on their northern border. Livy notes them on Hannibal's route through the Alps in 218 BCE.
allobroges.r: They were a warlike people governed by a nobility, rich in cattle and controlling routes into the Alps. In 123 BCE they sheltered Teutomalius, king of the Salyes, which gave Rome its pretext for war.
allobroges.e: Rome defeated them in 121 BCE, and their land became part of Gallia Narbonensis. In 63 BCE their envoys revealed Catiline's plot to Cicero, but in 61 BCE they rose under Catugnatus and were crushed. Vienne became a wealthy Roman colony.

alawite-state.t: A French-created state for the Alawite mountains and coast of Syria, separated from the rest of Syria between 1920 and 1936.
alawite-state.o: In 1920 France established the Territory of the Alawites, covering the coastal mountains and the port of Latakia, where the Alawites, a heterodox Shia community long marginalised under the Ottomans, were the majority in the countryside. The territory became the Alawite State in 1922.
alawite-state.r: Governed by French officials with an Alawite-dominated representative council, the state withdrew from the Syrian Federation in 1924 and was renamed the Government of Latakia in 1930. France recruited many Alawites into its colonial army. Road-building and land reform were undertaken, but the coastal towns, largely Sunni and Christian, favoured union with Syria.
alawite-state.e: Under the 1936 Franco-Syrian treaty the state was incorporated into the Syrian Republic, despite petitions by some Alawite notables asking to remain separate, and it was fully integrated in 1937.

autonomous-governorate-of-estonia.t: Self-governing Estonian province created by Russia's Provisional Government in 1917, whose assembly prepared the declaration of Estonian independence.
autonomous-governorate-of-estonia.o: After the February Revolution, Russia's Provisional Government decreed on 12 April 1917 that the Governorate of Estonia would be joined with the Estonian-speaking northern districts of the Governorate of Livonia, uniting the Estonian people in one autonomous province. Jaan Poska, mayor of Reval, became its commissar.
autonomous-governorate-of-estonia.r: For the first time Estonians governed their own land. An elected provincial assembly, the Maapäev, met in July 1917, and a Provincial Government led by Konstantin Päts was formed. Estonian replaced German as the language of administration, and national regiments were organised.
autonomous-governorate-of-estonia.e: After the Bolshevik coup, the Maapäev declared itself the sovereign power in Estonia on 28 November 1917 before being dispersed by local Bolsheviks. As German troops advanced and the Bolsheviks withdrew, the Salvation Committee declared the Republic of Estonia on 24 February 1918; the Germans then occupied the country until November.

autonomous-albanian-republic-of-korce.t: Albanian autonomous region set up under French military protection during the First World War, which gave Korçë its own schools, money and stamps.
autonomous-albanian-republic-of-korce.o: During the First World War French forces of the Salonika front occupied Korçë in late 1916. To secure the area against Greek irregulars and win local support, the French commander signed the Protocol of Korçë in December 1916 with Albanian notables, creating an autonomous Albanian province under French protection, with Themistokli Gërmenji as prefect of police.
autonomous-albanian-republic-of-korce.r: A council of Christian and Muslim Albanian representatives ran the town and surrounding villages, and Albanian became the language of administration and schools, including the first Albanian secular secondary school. The republic issued its own stamps and banknotes and flew an Albanian flag with French colours. Real authority lay with the French army.
autonomous-albanian-republic-of-korce.e: France ended the autonomy in February 1918 and governed the district militarily, Gërmenji having been executed by a French court in 1917. In 1920 French troops withdrew and handed Korçë to the Albanian government created at Lushnjë, ensuring it stayed in Albania rather than Greece.

allied-occupied-germany.t: Defeated Germany under the rule of the four Allied powers, divided into zones that grew into two German states.
allied-occupied-germany.o: After Germany's unconditional surrender in May 1945, the Berlin Declaration of 5 June 1945 transferred supreme authority to the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and France. Germany was divided into four occupation zones, Berlin into four sectors, and the lands east of the Oder-Neisse line passed to Polish and Soviet administration.
allied-occupied-germany.r: The Allied Control Council coordinated policy under the Potsdam Agreement: denazification, demilitarisation, democratisation and reparations. The major Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg. Millions of Germans expelled from the east had to be resettled. Cooperation broke down as the Cold War began: the western zones introduced the Deutsche Mark in 1948, and the Soviets blockaded West Berlin, answered by the Berlin Airlift.
allied-occupied-germany.e: In May 1949 the western zones became the Federal Republic of Germany, and in October 1949 the Soviet zone became the German Democratic Republic. Allied rights over Germany as a whole ended only with reunification in 1990.

agder.t: Petty kingdom on Norway's southern tip whose king, according to the sagas, fought Harald Fairhair at Hafrsfjord.
agder.o: Agder, the southernmost coast of Norway, was a small kingdom in the Viking Age. The sagas link it with the Vestfold dynasty through Queen Åsa, daughter of a king of Agder and mother of Halfdan the Black.
agder.r: Agder faced the Skagerrak and Denmark and lived by farming, fishing and sea trade. Its rulers are known only from late saga tradition, and the boundaries of the kingdom are uncertain.
agder.e: Heimskringla says that Kjotve the Rich, king of Agder, joined the western coalition defeated by Harald Fairhair at Hafrsfjord, traditionally around 872. Agder then passed into the Kingdom of Norway.

alaiye-beylik.t: A small Turkish principality at Alanya on the Mediterranean coast, ruled by a branch of the Karamanids under the great Seljuk citadel.
alaiye-beylik.o: Alanya was built up by the Seljuk sultan Kayqubad I after 1221 as a winter capital and naval base. After Seljuk authority collapsed in the late 13th century, local Turkish lords, later linked to the Karamanids, took over the city and its surrounding coast.
alaiye-beylik.r: The rulers lived in the Seljuk citadel and used its shipyard and Red Tower. Ibn Battuta visited in the 1330s and met its ruler Yusuf Bey. The town traded timber and other goods with Cyprus, Egypt and Venice. In 1427 its ruler sold Alanya to the Mamluk sultan Barsbay, though Mamluk control did not last, and the Karamanid line returned.
alaiye-beylik.e: The Ottoman commander Gedik Ahmed Pasha took Alanya in 1471 from its last ruler, Kilij Arslan, who received a domain elsewhere.

aulerci-eburovices.t: Branch of the Aulerci around Évreux in Normandy who killed their own council rather than stay out of the war against Caesar.
aulerci-eburovices.o: The Eburovices were part of the Aulerci group of peoples and held the land between the Seine and the Eure, around the oppidum later called Mediolanum Aulercorum.
aulerci-eburovices.r: Caesar records that in 56 BCE they and the Lexovii murdered their senators, who opposed war, and joined the coalition of Viridovix of the Unelli. The episode shows that they were governed by a council of nobles.
aulerci-eburovices.e: The coalition was defeated by Quintus Titurius Sabinus in 56 BCE, and the Eburovices joined the general revolt again in 52 BCE. Under Rome Mediolanum Aulercorum became a civitas capital, the origin of Évreux.

alemanni.t: A confederation of Germanic peoples on the upper Rhine and Danube that overran Rome's Agri Decumates and gave its name to Germany in French and Spanish.
alemanni.o: The Alemanni ('all men') are first named in 213, when Caracalla fought them on the Main. They formed from Elbe Germanic groups, including Suebian peoples such as the Semnones, who moved towards the Roman frontier. After the Limes collapsed around 260 they settled the land between the upper Rhine, the Danube and Lake Constance.
alemanni.r: The Alemanni had no single king but many regional kings and princes who sometimes joined forces. They raided Gaul and Italy repeatedly; Julian defeated a coalition under Chnodomar at Strasbourg in 357. Many Alemanni also served in the Roman army. They lived in farmsteads and hilltop centres such as the Runder Berg near Urach.
alemanni.e: Clovis I and the Franks defeated the Alemanni at Tolbiac around 496 and again around 506. Some came under Ostrogothic protection, but by 536 all were under Frankish rule, forming the Duchy of Alamannia. Their dialects survive as Alemannic German in Swabia, Alsace and Switzerland.

ayyubid-emirate-of-homs.t: An Ayyubid principality of the descendants of Shirkuh, whose last prince helped defeat the Mongols at the first battle of Homs in 1260.
ayyubid-emirate-of-homs.o: In 1179 Saladin granted Homs to his cousin Nasir al-Din Muhammad, son of Shirkuh, the uncle who had conquered Egypt. The town remained with this line of the family as a hereditary principality.
ayyubid-emirate-of-homs.r: Homs guarded the gap between the coast and the interior and faced the County of Tripoli and the Nizari castles. Asad al-Din Shirkuh II ruled for over fifty years (1186-1240), keeping the town through shifting alliances. His successor al-Mansur Ibrahim fought alongside the Franks against Egypt and lost at La Forbie in 1244. Al-Ashraf Musa lost Homs for a time to Aleppo.
ayyubid-emirate-of-homs.e: Al-Ashraf Musa, restored by the Mongols, switched sides and with Mamluk troops defeated a Mongol army at Homs in December 1260. After his death in 1262, the Mamluk sultan Baybars annexed the principality.

albanian-republic.t: Albania's first republic, a presidential regime built by Ahmet Zogu that drew the country closely towards Fascist Italy.
albanian-republic.o: Ahmet Zogu, a chieftain from Mat, was driven out by Fan Noli's June Revolution of 1924 but returned in December with support from the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and White Russian mercenaries. In January 1925 a constituent assembly abolished the Principality of Albania and proclaimed a republic with Tirana as capital, electing Zogu president for seven years.
albanian-republic.r: The 1925 statute gave the president sweeping powers over the government, army and legislation. Zogu disarmed clans, suppressed opponents and built roads and a gendarmerie. Short of money, he turned to Italy: an Italian-controlled national bank and development company were founded, and the Treaties of Tirana of 1926 and 1927 made Albania an Italian ally.
albanian-republic.e: On 1 September 1928 a constituent assembly proclaimed Albania a monarchy, and Zogu became King Zog I of the Albanian Kingdom. The new constitution kept much of the presidential system but made the office hereditary, and the dependence on Italian money continued.
albanian-republic.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

albanian-kingdom.t: Albania's only native monarchy, the kingdom of Zog I, which modernised the country's laws while falling ever deeper under Italian control.
albanian-kingdom.o: On 1 September 1928 a constituent assembly turned the Albanian Republic into a kingdom, and President Ahmet Zogu became Zog I, King of the Albanians, a title chosen to suggest claims beyond the state's borders. Tirana remained the capital, and the strong presidential powers of 1925 passed to the crown.
albanian-kingdom.r: Zog ruled as an authoritarian moderniser, introducing civil and penal codes based on Italian, French and Swiss models, separating religion from the state and banning the face veil in 1937. Schools, roads and a small army were built, largely with Italian loans and advisers, and Italy controlled the oil concessions and the national bank. Revolts, such as that at Fier in 1935, were suppressed.
albanian-kingdom.e: Mussolini invaded on 7 April 1939, and resistance collapsed within days. Zog fled with Queen Geraldine and their newborn son, never to return. Italy turned the country into the Albanian Kingdom (1939-1943) under King Victor Emmanuel III.
albanian-kingdom.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

andosini.t: A Pyrenean people subdued by Hannibal on his march to Italy in 218 BCE, often linked with the name of Andorra.
andosini.o: The Andosini are known only from Polybius, who lists them among the peoples between the Ebro and the Pyrenees that Hannibal conquered in 218 BCE. They are usually placed in the high valleys around modern Andorra, whose name is often thought to derive from theirs.
andosini.r: Nothing is known of their society beyond a probable mountain economy of herding and small-scale farming.
andosini.e: After Hannibal's campaign their territory was left under the Carthaginian officer Hanno. Following the Roman victories in the north-east and Cato's campaign of 195 BCE, the area passed into Hispania Citerior, and the Andosini are not mentioned again.

ambarri.t: Gallic people of the lower Saône and Ain, clients of the Aedui whose appeal for help helped draw Caesar into Gaul in 58 BCE.
ambarri.o: Their name means those on both sides of the Arar, the ancient Saône. Livy lists the Ambarri among the peoples who followed Bellovesus into northern Italy in the legendary migrations of around 600 BCE. In Caesar's day they lived east of the Saône, near the Rhône confluence.
ambarri.r: Caesar calls them friends and kinsmen of the Aedui, on whom they depended. No rulers or towns are recorded.
ambarri.e: When the migrating Helvetii plundered their fields in 58 BCE, the Ambarri complained to Caesar, adding to his reasons to attack. After the conquest their territory was divided among neighbouring civitates, and the name survives only in a few place names in the Ain.

aram-damascus.t: Aram-Damascus, the strongest Aramaean kingdom, which led Syria against Assyria and dominated Israel under King Hazael.
aram-damascus.o: After the Late Bronze Age, Aramaean groups took over the Damascus oasis, once Egyptian Upi. The Bible credits Rezon, a fugitive officer of Aram-Zobah, with founding the kingdom in the 10th century BCE, and under Ben-Hadad I it became the leading power of southern Syria.
aram-damascus.r: Its kings ruled from Damascus over the oasis and the Hauran, controlling caravan routes from Arabia. Hadadezer led the coalition with Hamath and the Kingdom of Israel against Shalmaneser III at Qarqar in 853 BCE. The usurper Hazael then conquered much of Israel and destroyed Gath; the Tel Dan stele probably records his victories.
aram-damascus.e: King Rezin allied with Israel against Judah, whose king appealed to Tiglath-Pileser III of the Assyrian Empire. The Assyrians took Damascus in 732 BCE, killed Rezin and made Aram an Assyrian province.

ambiani.t: Belgic people of the Somme valley whose town Samarobriva, modern Amiens, hosted Caesar's council of Gaul in 54 BCE.
ambiani.o: The Ambiani held the lower and middle Somme in Picardy. Caesar records that they promised ten thousand warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE and surrendered after the league broke up.
ambiani.r: Their oppidum of Samarobriva, the bridge on the Samara or Somme, controlled a key crossing. They struck abundant gold coins, some of the earliest in northern Gaul.
ambiani.e: Caesar held an assembly of the Gallic peoples at Samarobriva in 54 BCE and wintered there. The Ambiani sent men to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE and fought again in 51 BCE. Under Rome Samarobriva became a major city, later Ambianum, the origin of Amiens.

autariatae.t: Large Illyrian tribal people of the central Balkans who overpowered the Triballi before being broken by Celtic invaders and Macedon.
autariatae.o: The Autariatae lived in the upper Drina and Lim valleys, in modern western Serbia, Bosnia and Montenegro, by the 5th century BCE. Strabo calls them once the greatest and best of the Illyrians.
autariatae.r: Little is known of their government; they appear as a warrior people of the interior. They fought their neighbours the Ardiaei over salt springs, and in the 4th century BCE defeated the Triballi and pushed east.
autariatae.e: Around 310 BCE Celtic incursions and a plague weakened them, and the Macedonian king Cassander resettled some 20,000 of them near Mount Orbelus. Their remnants were absorbed by the Scordisci and other neighbours, and the name disappears in the 3rd century BCE.

alan-kingdom-in-hispania.t: The short-lived realm of the Iranian-speaking Alans in Lusitania and Carthaginiensis, destroyed by the Visigoths within a decade.
alan-kingdom-in-hispania.o: The Alans, nomads from the steppe north of the Caucasus, crossed the Rhine in 406 with Vandals and Suebi and entered Hispania in 409. In 411, when the invaders divided the provinces by lot, the Alans took Lusitania and Carthaginiensis, the largest share.
alan-kingdom-in-hispania.r: They formed a warrior aristocracy ruling over a Hispano-Roman population, living from tribute and plunder rather than building lasting institutions. Their king Addax led them in Hispania. Very little is known of their administration, and Hydatius is the main source.
alan-kingdom-in-hispania.e: From 416 the Visigothic king Wallia, acting for Rome, campaigned against them, and in 418 Addax was killed. The surviving Alans joined the Hasding Vandals under Gunderic, whose kings in Africa styled themselves kings of the Vandals and Alans.

amphipolis.t: Athenian colony on the Strymon river, key to the timber and gold of Thrace, whose loss to Sparta in 424 BCE exiled the historian Thucydides.
amphipolis.o: The site, a loop of the lower Strymon called Ennea Hodoi (Nine Ways), had long attracted Athens; a first attempt to settle it ended in disaster around 465 BCE. In 437 BCE Hagnon founded Amphipolis there with Athenian and allied settlers, controlling the river crossing and the route to the timber and gold and silver mines of Mount Pangaion.
amphipolis.r: Amphipolis was a mixed community in which Athenians were a minority among other Greek settlers, which weakened loyalty to Athens. It governed itself through an assembly and magistrates, honoured Hagnon as founder and later the Spartan Brasidas, and grew rich on timber for shipbuilding, precious metals and trade with Thrace and Macedon.
amphipolis.e: Brasidas captured it in 424 BCE; both he and the Athenian Cleon died in battle there in 422 BCE. Independent afterwards and never recovered by Athens, it fell to Philip II in 357 BCE. It became a leading Macedonian city and mint, and in 167 BCE capital of one of the Four Macedonian Republics.

aetolian-league.t: Federal state of the Aetolians of west-central Greece that became one of the great powers of Hellenistic Greece and controlled the oracle of Delphi.
aetolian-league.o: The Aetolians lived in mountain villages north of the Gulf of Corinth, scorned by Thucydides as primitive. By 367 BCE an Aetolian federation was acting as a state, with its religious centre at the sanctuary of Apollo at Thermon. Its prestige soared when it helped repel the Gallic invasion of Delphi in 279 BCE.
aetolian-league.r: The league had a general assembly of all citizens meeting at Thermon and elsewhere, a large council and an annual general (strategos) assisted by a committee, the apokletoi. It expanded by granting citizenship or alliance to distant cities, controlled the votes of the Amphictyonic League and was notorious for licensed raiding and piracy. Leaders such as Dorimachus and Scopas fought Philip V of Macedon.
aetolian-league.e: Allied with Rome against Philip V in 211 BCE, the Aetolians felt cheated after Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE and invited Antiochus III to Greece. Defeated at Thermopylae in 191 BCE, the league accepted a peace in 189 BCE that left it a subordinate ally of Rome.

al-andalus-umayyad-province.t: Iberia as a province of the Umayyad Caliphate of Damascus, ruled by governors from 711 until Abd al-Rahman I founded an independent emirate.
al-andalus-umayyad-province.o: In 711 Tariq ibn Ziyad crossed from North Africa with a mainly Berber army and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic near the Guadalete. His superior Musa ibn Nusayr followed in 712, and within a few years most of the peninsula had been conquered, often by treaties with local lords such as Theodemir of Tudmir.
al-andalus-umayyad-province.r: Al-Andalus was governed by walis appointed from Kairouan or Damascus, first from Seville and from around 716 from Córdoba. Christians and Jews kept their faith in return for tribute. Raids pushed into Gaul until Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was defeated near Poitiers in 732. Tensions between Arabs and Berbers erupted in the Berber revolt of 740, after which Syrian troops under Balj settled in the south.
al-andalus-umayyad-province.e: Rival Arab factions fought for power in the 740s and 750s. After the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750, the Umayyad prince Abd al-Rahman reached al-Andalus, took Córdoba in 756 and founded the Emirate of Córdoba.

alempois.t: One of the smallest ancient Estonian lands, a district of central Estonia known only from the chronicle of the Livonian crusade.
alempois.o: Alempois appears in Henry of Livonia's chronicle as a small Estonian district near Sakala and Nurmekund in central Estonia. Its exact boundaries are uncertain.
alempois.r: It probably consisted of one or two parishes led by elders and shared the culture of the neighbouring Estonian counties. Nothing else is reliably known.
alempois.e: Alempois was taken during the crusaders' conquest of Estonia, completed in 1224, and came under the Livonian Brothers of the Sword and later the Livonian Order.

apollonia-pontica.t: Milesian colony on the Black Sea coast of Thrace whose colossal statue of Apollo was carried off to Rome in 72 BCE.
apollonia-pontica.o: Settlers from Miletus founded Apollonia c. 610 BCE on a peninsula and island on the western Black Sea coast, at modern Sozopol in Bulgaria. Named after Apollo, it became one of the leading Greek cities of the Thracian coast.
apollonia-pontica.r: Apollonia traded wine, oil and fine pottery with the Thracians, including the Odrysian Kingdom, for grain, metals and honey. Its coins carried an anchor. In the 5th century BCE it set up a bronze statue of Apollo by Calamis, about 13 metres high. It was governed as an oligarchy and later a democracy.
apollonia-pontica.e: In 72 BCE Marcus Lucullus captured Apollonia during the Third Mithridatic War and took the Apollo statue to the Capitol in Rome. The city then came under Roman control and survives as Sozopol.

arevaci.t: The strongest of the Celtiberian peoples, defenders of Numantia, whose siege by Scipio Aemilianus in 134 to 133 BCE became a byword for resistance.
arevaci.o: The Arevaci occupied the upper Douro basin in modern Soria and Segovia from about the 4th century BCE. Strabo called them the most powerful of the Celtiberians, and their towns included Numantia, Termes and Uxama.
arevaci.r: They lived in large fortified towns with grid-like streets, governed by councils and elected war leaders. Numantia's pottery shows painted horses and warriors. Herding, cereal growing and iron working sustained them, and their warriors were renowned in Roman sources for courage and skill with the sword.
arevaci.e: From 153 BCE they led resistance to Rome, defeating several consuls. In 134 BCE Scipio Aemilianus surrounded Numantia with walls and starved it; Retogenes broke out to seek aid, but the town fell in 133 BCE. The Arevaci later backed Sertorius before becoming part of Hispania Citerior.

astrakhan-khanate.t: A Tatar khanate at the mouth of the Volga, a successor of the Golden Horde whose annexation in 1556 gave Russia the whole Volga route.
astrakhan-khanate.o: The Astrakhan Khanate formed in the 1460s around the town of Xacitarxan near the Volga delta, under khans descended from Küchük Muhammad of the Great Horde. It became fully independent after the Great Horde's destruction in 1502.
astrakhan-khanate.r: The khanate was small and relatively weak, controlling the fisheries and trade of the lower Volga, including the caravan routes towards the Caspian and Persia. Its population of Tatars and Nogais lived largely by herding and trade. Its khans were frequently dependent on the Nogai Horde or the Crimean Khanate, and several were installed by these neighbours.
astrakhan-khanate.e: After taking Kazan, Ivan IV turned south: Russian forces installed a client khan, Dervish Ali, in 1554 and annexed the khanate in 1556. Astrakhan became a Russian fortress city and gateway to the Caspian and the Caucasus.

ayyubid-emirate-of-aleppo.t: The Ayyubid principality of northern Syria whose rulers built much of the Citadel of Aleppo as it stands today.
ayyubid-emirate-of-aleppo.o: Saladin took Aleppo from the Zengids in 1183 and in 1186 gave it to his son al-Zahir Ghazi, whose line ruled it until the Mongol invasion.
ayyubid-emirate-of-aleppo.r: Al-Zahir Ghazi rebuilt the Citadel of Aleppo with its sloping glacis, monumental gate and water supply, and endowed madrasas. His widow Dayfa Khatun, a niece of Saladin, governed as regent from 1236 to 1242, one of the few women to rule in medieval Syria, and founded the Firdaws madrasa. Aleppo kept treaties with Venice and the Principality of Antioch and flourished on trade. Al-Nasir Yusuf took Damascus in 1250, ruling most of Syria.
ayyubid-emirate-of-aleppo.e: Hulagu's Mongols stormed Aleppo in January 1260 and massacred many inhabitants. Al-Nasir Yusuf fled, was captured and was later killed by the Mongols. After Ain Jalut, Aleppo passed to the Mamluks.

aksumite-yemen.t: Yemen under Ethiopian Christian rule, best known for Abraha, who repaired the Marib Dam and, by tradition, marched on Mecca with an elephant.
aksumite-yemen.o: In 525 the Aksumite Empire under King Kaleb crossed the Red Sea to avenge the Christians of Najran, defeated the Himyarite king Yusuf and installed Sumyafa Ashwa, a local Christian, as viceroy. Within a few years the Aksumite general Abraha overthrew him and made himself ruler, nominally under Aksum.
aksumite-yemen.r: Abraha governed in practice independently from Sanaa. His inscriptions record the restoration of the Marib Dam in 548 and a diplomatic conference attended by envoys of the Byzantine Empire, Persia and the Arab kings. He built a great church in Sanaa and campaigned deep into central Arabia; Muslim tradition remembers his failed expedition against Mecca in the Year of the Elephant.
aksumite-yemen.e: Abraha's sons Yaksum and Masruq were unpopular. The Himyarite noble Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan sought help from Persia, and around 570 a Sasanian force under Wahriz defeated the Ethiopians, opening the period of Sasanian Yemen.

aq-qoyunlu.t: The 'White Sheep' Turkmen confederation that rose from Diyarbakir to rule Iran under Uzun Hasan before giving way to the Safavids.
aq-qoyunlu.o: The Aq Qoyunlu were led by the Bayandur clan among the Turkmen tribes pasturing around Diyarbakir in the late 14th century. Their chief Qara Yuluk Osman fought the Kadi Burhan al-Din state and the Qara Qoyunlu, sided with Timur, and was rewarded with Diyarbakir.
aq-qoyunlu.r: Uzun Hasan defeated the Qara Qoyunlu ruler Jahan Shah in 1467 and the Timurid Abu Sa'id in 1469, making Tabriz his capital and ruling Iran, Iraq and eastern Anatolia. He allied with Venice against the Ottomans, but Mehmed II defeated him at Otlukbeli in 1473. His son Ya'qub kept a Persianate court that patronised poets and painters, while tribal chiefs held real military power.
aq-qoyunlu.e: After Ya'qub's death in 1490 the confederation split among rival princes. Ismail, grandson of Uzun Hasan through his daughter, defeated them in 1501 and founded the Safavid state; the last Aq Qoyunlu ruler, Murad, was driven out in 1503.

arab-byzantine-condominium-of-cyprus.t: Nearly three centuries in which Cyprus was neutral ground shared between the Byzantine Empire and the Caliphate, which split its taxes.
arab-byzantine-condominium-of-cyprus.o: Arab fleets raided Cyprus from 649. In 688 the Byzantine emperor Justinian II and the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik agreed a treaty under which the revenues of Cyprus, along with those of Armenia and Iberia, were divided equally between them. The island was to be demilitarised and neutral, though the arrangement was repeatedly interrupted.
arab-byzantine-condominium-of-cyprus.r: Cyprus kept its Greek-speaking Christian population, its bishops and local officials, while paying tribute to both powers. Justinian II moved many islanders to Cyzicus around 691, and they returned about 698. Both sides violated the neutrality: Byzantine and Abbasid fleets raided the island, and Harun al-Rashid's forces deported Cypriots. Historians debate how formal the condominium really was.
arab-byzantine-condominium-of-cyprus.e: As Byzantine power revived in the 10th century, Nikephoros II Phokas sent the patrician Niketas Chalkoutzes to retake Cyprus in 965. It became a Byzantine province until Isaac Komnenos seized it in 1184.

appenzell-ausserrhoden.t: The Reformed half of Appenzell, created in 1597, which became one of the most industrialised rural areas of early modern Europe.
appenzell-ausserrhoden.o: When the Canton of Appenzell was divided in 1597, the outer districts, which had adopted the Reformed faith, formed Ausserrhoden. Without the old capital, its Landsgemeinde met alternately in Trogen and Hundwil, and government business was shared between Trogen and Herisau.
appenzell-ausserrhoden.r: From the 17th century the villagers spun and wove linen and later cotton at home, and merchant families such as the Zellwegers of Trogen grew rich in international trade. Government lay with the Landsgemeinde and councils, and the half-canton shared a vote with Innerrhoden at the federal Diet.
appenzell-ausserrhoden.e: In 1798 it was absorbed into the canton of Säntis of the Helvetic Republic, and in 1803 it was restored as a half-canton. Ausserrhoden abolished its Landsgemeinde in 1997 and remains a Swiss canton.

azzi-hayasa.t: Azzi-Hayasa, a mountain confederation of north-eastern Anatolia that fought the Hittites in the 14th century BCE.
azzi-hayasa.o: Hayasa and Azzi were lands in the highlands of the upper Euphrates and the Erzurum region. They appear in Hittite records from the 15th century BCE as a federation of mountain communities beyond the Hittite frontier.
azzi-hayasa.r: Little is known of its internal structure. Suppiluliuma I of the Hittite Empire made a treaty with Hukkana of Hayasa and gave him his sister in marriage, with strict rules about Hittite customs. Some scholars connect Hayasa with the Armenian name for Armenia, Hay, though this is disputed.
azzi-hayasa.e: Mursili II fought Anniya of Azzi in long campaigns, and Hayasa disappears from the record in the 13th century BCE. The highlands later formed part of Nairi and the Kingdom of Urartu.

austrian-delagoa-bay.t: The Habsburg monarchy's only African colony, a brief trading venture on Delagoa Bay led by the adventurer William Bolts.
austrian-delagoa-bay.o: William Bolts, a former East India Company servant, persuaded the Austrian government of Maria Theresa to back a trading venture to the East under the imperial flag. In 1777 he landed at Delagoa Bay and signed agreements with local Tsonga rulers, including the Tembe Kingdom, to establish trading posts.
austrian-delagoa-bay.r: The Austrian posts, run by agents of Bolts's company and later the Imperial Asiatic Company of Trieste, traded cloth and metal goods for ivory. The settlement was tiny and dependent on the goodwill of local rulers, and it was meant to link Austrian trade with India and China.
austrian-delagoa-bay.e: Portugal, which claimed the bay, sent a naval force in 1781 that expelled the Austrians and built a fort. Bolts's company soon failed, and Austria made no further colonial attempts in Africa.

acarnanian-league.t: Federation of the Acarnanian towns of western Greece, a long-standing enemy of the Aetolians and an ally first of Athens and later of Macedon.
acarnanian-league.o: Acarnania, between the Ambracian Gulf and the Achelous river, was a land of small towns and villages. By the mid-5th century BCE they were acting together as a league with its meeting place at Stratos. Hostility to Corinth's colonies in the region pushed them into alliance with Athens, whose general Phormio campaigned with them in the Peloponnesian War.
acarnanian-league.r: The league had a federal assembly, council and elected general (strategos), and struck federal coins. Its members were mainly farmers and herders known as skilled slingers and fighters. Ancient writers considered the Acarnanians conservative and fiercely loyal to allies, especially in their long struggle against the expanding Aetolian League.
acarnanian-league.e: Aetolia and Epirus partitioned Acarnania in the mid-3rd century BCE, but the league was restored around 230 BCE and sided with Macedon. Rome detached Leucas and made it the federal capital in 197 BCE. The league faded under Roman rule; after Actium in 31 BCE Augustus moved much of its population to his new city of Nicopolis.

albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.t: Nominally independent Albanian state set up by Germany after Italy's surrender in 1943, which kept Kosovo but was defeated by the Communist Partisans.
albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.o: When Italy capitulated in September 1943, German troops occupied the Albanian Kingdom (1939-1943). Seeking local support, Germany declared Albania independent, convened a national assembly and set up a Regency Council headed by Mehdi Frashëri, with Albanian governments led successively by figures such as Rexhep Mitrovica.
albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.r: The regime claimed neutrality and kept the Albanian-inhabited lands of Kosovo and western Macedonia added in 1941, while Germany controlled the military situation. Some nationalists of the Balli Kombëtar cooperated with the Germans against the Partisans, and an SS division was recruited in Kosovo. Many Jews in Albania were sheltered by Albanian families and survived.
albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.e: Enver Hoxha's Partisans won the civil war and took Tirana on 17 November 1944 as German forces withdrew. The communists then founded what became the People's Socialist Republic of Albania, and Kosovo returned to Yugoslavia.
albanian-kingdom-1943-1944.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

akatziri.t: A steppe people north of the Black Sea who were drawn into Attila's empire and later appear among the forerunners of the Khazars.
akatziri.o: The Akatziri are first mentioned by the Byzantine envoy Priscus in the 440s as a people of the Pontic steppe ruled by many chiefs. Jordanes later described them as a strong people who lived by herding and hunting. Their origins and language are unknown; they were probably a Hunnic or early Turkic group.
akatziri.r: Around 448 the Eastern Roman emperor Theodosius II tried to bribe their chiefs to turn against Attila, but the gifts went to the wrong chief, Kuridachus, who betrayed the plan. Attila then subdued them and set his eldest son Ellac over them as king, bringing them firmly into the Hunnic Empire.
akatziri.e: After the collapse of Hun power in the 450s and 460s, the Akatziri disappear from the record, displaced or absorbed by the Saragurs, Sabirs and Onogurs. Some historians link them to the later Khazars, though the connection is unproven.

aqrabi-sheikhdom.t: A tiny sheikhdom west of Aden whose land included the peninsula where Britain built the Little Aden oil refinery.
aqrabi-sheikhdom.o: The Aqrabi tribe held a small coastal district west of Aden, with its seat at Bir Ahmad. They broke from the neighbouring Sultanate of Lahej in the 18th century to form their own sheikhdom. Its early history is poorly known.
aqrabi-sheikhdom.r: With only a few thousand inhabitants, the sheikhdom lived from farming, fishing and its position near Aden. In the 1860s Britain bought the Little Aden peninsula from the Aqrabi sheikh, and it became part of British Aden; a large oil refinery opened there in 1954. The sheikhdom was a British-protected state and joined the Federation of South Arabia.
aqrabi-sheikhdom.e: In 1967 the National Liberation Front took over, and the territory was incorporated into South Yemen.

achaemenid-egypt.t: Egypt as a satrapy of the Persian Empire, ruled by Persian kings who were also crowned as pharaohs.
achaemenid-egypt.o: In 525 BCE Cambyses II defeated Psamtik III of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty of Egypt at Pelusium and took Memphis, making Egypt a province of the Achaemenid Empire. Manetho counts the Persian kings as the Twenty-seventh Dynasty. The Egyptian official Udjahorresnet helped Cambyses adopt pharaonic titles.
achaemenid-egypt.r: A Persian satrap governed from Memphis, collecting tribute in grain and silver. Darius I had Egyptian laws collected, completed the Nile to Red Sea canal and built the temple of Hibis in the Kharga Oasis. Aramaic served as the administrative language beside Egyptian, and a garrison of Jewish soldiers at Elephantine left a rich archive of Aramaic papyri. Revolts broke out in 486 BCE and under Inaros, who was supported by Athens, around 460 BCE.
achaemenid-egypt.e: After the death of Darius II, the Saite noble Amyrtaeus rebelled in 404 BCE and freed Egypt, founding the Twenty-eighth Dynasty of Egypt. Persia reconquered the country in 343 BCE.

ashdod.t: Ashdod, a Philistine city of the coastal plain, famed in the Bible for its temple of Dagon and later for revolt against Assyria.
ashdod.o: Ashdod had been a Canaanite town before Philistine newcomers settled there in the 12th century BCE, making it one of the cities of the Philistine Pentapolis. Excavations at Tel Ashdod uncovered Aegean-style pottery and figurines from this period.
ashdod.r: Its kings ruled the city and a harbour on the coast. The Bible tells of the Ark of the Covenant placed in its temple of Dagon. In 712 BCE King Yamani led a revolt against the Assyrian Empire, and Sargon II crushed it, setting up a victory stele in the city.
ashdod.e: Ashdod remained an Assyrian vassal, survived a long Egyptian siege under Psamtik I, and lost its kings to Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire, who deported them to Babylon c. 604 BCE.

aulerci-cenomani.t: Gallic people of Maine, centred on Le Mans, a branch of whom crossed the Alps and founded the Celtic towns of Brescia and Verona.
aulerci-cenomani.o: The Cenomani were the largest branch of the Aulerci and held the Sarthe valley around Vindinum (Le Mans). Livy and Polybius report that part of the people migrated across the Alps around 400 BCE and settled north of the Po, where the Italian Cenomani founded Brixia (Brescia) and became allies of Rome against the other Gauls.
aulerci-cenomani.r: Little is known of the Gallic Cenomani at home. They struck gold coins and controlled the route between the Loire and the Channel coast.
aulerci-cenomani.e: They joined the great revolt of 52 BCE and sent five thousand men to relieve Alesia. Under Rome Vindinum grew into a walled town, later called Civitas Cenomanorum, from which come the names Le Mans and Maine.

antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.t: Kingdom of the Antigonid dynasty, which ruled Macedon and dominated Greece for over a century until defeated by Rome at Pydna in 168 BCE.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.o: Antigonus I Monophthalmus and his son Demetrius Poliorcetes, generals of Alexander, took the royal title in 306 BCE while ruling in Asia. Demetrius seized Macedon in 294 BCE but lost it in 288 BCE. His son Antigonus II Gonatas won the throne after defeating the Gauls at Lysimachia in 277 BCE, founding a stable dynasty at Pella.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.r: Antigonid kings ruled Macedon directly through a landed aristocracy and a citizen army famous for its sarissa phalanx, while controlling Greece through garrisons at Corinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, the 'fetters of Greece'. They patronised philosophy and the arts. Antigonus III Doson formed a Hellenic alliance and defeated Sparta at Sellasia in 222 BCE.
antigonid-kingdom-of-macedonia.e: Philip V's alliance with Hannibal led to wars with Rome; defeat at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE confined him to Macedon. His son Perseus lost to Lucius Aemilius Paullus at Pydna in 168 BCE. Rome abolished the monarchy and divided the land into the Four Macedonian Republics.

aurunci.t: Ancient Italic people of the coast between Latium and Campania, whose towns were destroyed by Rome in 314 BCE.
aurunci.o: The Aurunci, called Ausones by the Greeks, lived between the Liri and Volturno rivers around the Roccamonfina volcano. Greek writers used 'Ausonia' for much of early Italy, which suggests they were once a widespread people. Little is known of their origins or language.
aurunci.r: Known only from Roman and Greek sources, the Aurunci lived in hill towns such as Ausona, Minturnae, Vescia and Suessa Aurunca. They fought Rome and the Latins in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, and later allied with the Sidicini against the Samnites.
aurunci.e: After they joined Rome's enemies during the Samnite Wars, Rome destroyed the towns of Ausona, Minturnae and Vescia in 314 BCE, massacring much of the population. Roman colonies followed at Suessa Aurunca in 313 BCE and Minturnae in 296 BCE, and the people disappeared from history.

acco.t: Acco, a Canaanite harbour town on the bay of Haifa, a vassal of Egypt in the Amarna age and forerunner of the later port of Acre.
acco.o: Akka grew on Tel Akko, beside the mouth of the Na'aman river, in the Middle Bronze Age, when it was surrounded by massive earth ramparts. It is named in Egyptian execration texts and in the list of towns conquered by Thutmose III.
acco.r: As a vassal of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom it was governed by local kings who traded with Cyprus and the Aegean through its harbour. Its rulers Zurata and Zatatna appear in the Amarna letters, accused by neighbours of plotting with Egypt's enemies.
acco.e: Acco's Canaanite kingdom ended in the upheavals of the 12th century BCE. The city later came under Phoenician rule, was renamed Ptolemais by the Ptolemaic Empire, and survives as Acre.

abdera.t: Thracian coastal city refounded by refugees from Teos, birthplace of the philosophers Democritus and Protagoras.
abdera.o: A first settlement at Abdera by Clazomenae c. 654 BCE was driven out by Thracians. Around 545 BCE citizens of Teos, fleeing the Persian general Harpagus, refounded the city on the Thracian coast east of the Nestos river.
abdera.r: Abdera grew rich from trade with the Thracian interior, minting silver coins with a griffin, and paid one of the highest tributes in the Delian League. It produced Democritus, founder of atomism, and the sophist Protagoras. Despite them, Abderites were the butt of Greek jokes about stupidity. The city was later under the influence of the Odrysian Kingdom.
abdera.e: Abdera was weakened by Thracian attacks in the 4th century BCE and annexed by Philip II of the Kingdom of Macedon c. 350 BCE. It survived under Macedonian, Ptolemaic and Roman rule as a smaller town.

apum.t: Apum, a north Mesopotamian kingdom ruling from Shamshi-Adad's former capital Shubat-Enlil, until Babylon destroyed it in 1728 BCE.
apum.o: Shubat-Enlil, at Tell Leilan in the Khabur plains, was the old city of Shehna, renamed by Shamshi-Adad as the capital of his Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia. After his death in the 1770s BCE his realm broke apart, and the city became the seat of the local kingdom of Apum.
apum.r: Its kings, such as Haya-abum and Till-Abnu, played the great powers against each other, and their palace archives at Tell Leilan preserve letters and treaties with Assur and other neighbours. The kingdom depended on rain-fed barley farming and the trade routes across the Khabur.
apum.e: The Babylonian Empire under Samsu-iluna, Hammurabi's son, sacked Shubat-Enlil in 1728 BCE and ended the kingdom. The city was abandoned, and excavations by Yale University from 1979 recovered its archives.
